entry.title: Renovate or Re-Platform? A Strategic Roadmap for Modernising Custom ABAP Applications
entry.content:
This blog walks through the full arc — from understanding the risk of legacy custom ABAP to making the renovate-or-re-platform decision and shaping a clean core strategy.

 

Legacy Custom Code - Strategic Risk

Across global enterprises, decades of classic ABAP custom code have accumulated in ECC and early S/4HANA implementations. This is not just a development concern — it is a strategic liability sitting at the heart of your business operations.

Two patterns dominate the field today. The first is brownfield carry-over: classic ABAP developments migrated from ECC to S/4HANA “as-is”, never re-evaluated against modern extensibility options. The system runs, but the architecture has not evolved. The second is greenfield but not clean: new S/4HANA implementations built with classic ABAP because project teams were unaware of — or not yet trained on — Clean Core tools such as ABAP Cloud, Key User Extensibility, and the RESTful Application Programming Model (RAP).

The cost of inaction compounds over time. Blocked upgrades. Rising maintenance spend. Incompatibility with cloud innovations — including embedded AI capabilities such as SAP Joule, which requires a clean, standard-aligned core to deliver its full value. With SAP’s continuous delivery model for S/4HANA Cloud and the end of mainstream maintenance for SAP Business Suite 7 approaching in 2027 (SAP Note 1648480), technical debt in custom ABAP is no longer a background risk — it is a front-line strategic concern.

 

What "Clean Core" Actually Means for Custom Extensions

“Clean Core” is one of the most frequently cited — and frequently misunderstood — concepts in the SAP ecosystem. Let us clarify: Clean Core is not about zero customisation. It is about smart, upgrade-stable customisation.

A system has a clean core when its custom extensions are decoupled from SAP standard code and interact with SAP business objects exclusively through well-defined, released interfaces. Extensions can still be rich, sophisticated, and deeply integrated — but they must not break during upgrades, and the upgrade cycle must not be broken by them.

SAP formalised this principle in August 2025 with the introduction of the Clean Core Level concept, classifying extensions into four maturity levels:

  • Level A — the cleanest: built on-stack with ABAP Cloud or side-by-side on SAP BTP — using the BTP ABAP Environment with RAP, SAP Build, CAP for Java/Node.js scenarios, or low-code/no-code tools. Fully upgrade-stable.
  • Level B — classic ABAP extensions using recommended classic APIs and accepted development technologies. Still considered clean core.
  • Level C — conditionally clean: extensions using internal SAP objects, acceptable only with additional governance checks (changelog for SAP objects) before upgrades.
  • Level D — not clean core: modifications, not-recommended SAP objects, implicit enhancements. These create direct upgrade risk.

This four-level model provides a practical maturity lens to classify the existing extension portfolio, define a clear target state, and proactively manage the risks associated with different clean core levels. The single source of truth for the classification criteria is SAP Note 3578329.

Key Reference:

• ABAP Extensibility Guide — Clean Core for SAP S/4HANA Cloud (August 2025)

 

The Strategic Decision: Renovate vs. Re-Platform

Here is one of the most persistent misconceptions in the field: Clean Core does not mean moving everything to SAP BTP. That oversimplification leads to poor architecture decisions, inflated costs, and unnecessary complexity.

The correct framing is a hybrid model — two complementary modernisation paths selected based on architectural coupling:

Approach

When to Apply

Target Platform

Renovate

Extension is tightly coupled to SAP standard processes, tables, or business objects

SAP S/4HANA core — using ABAP Cloud, Key User Extensibility, released BAdIs and APIs

Re-Platform

Extension is loosely coupled: standalone UIs, independent workflows, cross-system orchestration

SAP BTP — using CAP, BTP ABAP Environment, SAP Build, Event Mesh, Integration Suite

Hybrid

Most real-world scenarios

Combination of both platforms

Coupling is the decisive factor — not preference, convenience, or team familiarity. As a general principle, extensions that are tightly coupled to SAP standard business objects and data models tend to stay on the S/4HANA core, while standalone applications and cross-system integrations are natural candidates for SAP BTP. However, the right placement depends on the specific coupling characteristics of each extension — a structured assessment using AEM helps determine this for each use case.

Getting this distinction right at the architectural level is where the real value lies — and it is exactly what the SAP Application Extension Methodology is designed to support.

 

The SAP Application Extension Methodology (AEM): A Structured Decision Framework

Making the renovate-vs-re-platform decision systematic and repeatable — rather than relying on tribal knowledge or ad-hoc judgment — requires a structured methodology. That is precisely what the SAP Application Extension Methodology (AEM) provides.

AEM is a structured, technology-agnostic methodology for assessing extension use cases and defining a target clean solution architecture. It is available on the SAP Help Portal with downloadable templates and can be applied to individual use cases or as a broader governance framework.

The methodology follows three phases, each producing documented, reusable outputs:

  1. Assess the Use Case — Align all stakeholders on the systems landscape, business context, and requirements before any technology decision is made.
  2. Classify Extension Tasks — Break the use case into technology-agnostic tasks by extension style (presentation, application, and data tier) and map each task to its natural domain.
  3. Define the Target Architecture — Map tasks to specific technologies and document the implementation roadmap. With AEM v2.4, each Technical Extension Building Block is tagged with a Clean Core Level (A–D), making the assessment directly traceable to SAP’s extensibility governance model.

AEM creates a shared language across business, functional, and technical stakeholders. Its templates are reusable across multiple renovation projects, forming the basis for an enterprise-wide extension governance framework.

Key References:

• Introducing SAP Application Extension Methodology v2.4 — SAP Community Blog

• SAP Help Portal — AEM Overview

 

Key Pre-Conditions and Governance Concerns

Before launching a renovation initiative, four prerequisites must be in place. Treat these as gates — not optional considerations.

Prerequisite 1 — S/4HANA first. Renovation and re-platforming are S/4HANA concerns. Clean Core tools — ABAP Cloud, Key User Extensibility, RAP — are not available on ECC. An S/4HANA transformation project must be in place or completed before meaningful extension modernisation can begin.

Prerequisite 2 — Fit-to-Standard before building. Confirm the requirement is a genuine gap. Never invest in renovating a custom extension that replicates functionality already delivered by SAP standard. Every renovation candidate must pass a fit-to-standard check first.

Prerequisite 3 — One use case at a time. This is not a bulk “lift and shift” exercise. Each renovation effort should focus on a single, well-scoped business use case. System-wide custom code portfolio analysis is a separate — and equally important — exercise (see SAP Intelligent Custom Code Management).

Prerequisite 4 — Build the knowledge baseline. Teams need a working understanding of S/4HANA extensibility options and BTP capabilities before architectural decisions can be made. SAP offers dedicated enablement workshops as a recommended starting point.

Governance angle:

  • AEM’s templates and decision rationale documentation serve as the foundation for an extension governance framework — ensuring consistent, auditable, and repeatable decisions across all renovation projects in an enterprise program.
  • SAP Activate underpins a clean core journey by combining prescriptive methodology, standardized content, and governance-ready tooling to help customers adopt and run standard capabilities, minimize modifications, and guide compliant extensibility throughout the lifecycle.

 

The Renovation Journey: Major Steps

The following roadmap outlines the major milestones from initial knowledge-building to a production-ready clean architecture:

  1. Build the knowledge foundation — Understand Clean Core, ABAP Cloud, Key User Extensibility, RAP, and SAP BTP extension options. SAP offers enablement workshops to align all project stakeholders on the art of the possible.
  2. Analyse the custom code landscape — Use SAP Intelligent Custom Code Management (ICCM) to gain transparency over the existing portfolio and classify custom objects by business relevance, upgrade risk, and renovation potential.
  3. Prioritise use cases — Select renovation candidates based on business value, upgrade risk, and architectural complexity. Use the clustering results, which is an output of ICCM, as prioritisation input.
  4. Assess and design using AEM — SAP provides structured analysis and architecture design workshops using the Application Extension Methodology, delivering a validated target architecture and implementation roadmap.
  5. Validate the results — Review technology recommendations, decision rationale, and the target solution architecture with all stakeholders before proceeding to implementation.
  6. Build or commission the solution — Implementation of the clean target architecture, optionally supported by SAP advisory services including Proof-of-Concept (PoC) engagements for technically complex scenarios.

 

What the Target Architecture Looks Like

A renovated, Clean Core-compliant solution architecture typically follows a hybrid pattern: S/4HANA core and SAP BTP working in concert, with a clear separation of concerns and well-defined integration boundaries.

On the S/4HANA core:

  • Key User Extensibility — custom fields, custom logic, and custom business objects created through in-app tools, without writing code
  • Developer Extensibility via ABAP Cloud / RAP — upgrade-stable extensions using only released APIs, BAdIs, and extension points
  • Data model extensions through released CDS view extensions

On SAP BTP:

  • New SAP Fiori / SAPUI5 applications replacing legacy SAP GUI / ALV-based interfaces
  • Loosely coupled business logic built with CAP on Cloud Foundry or in the BTP ABAP Environment using RAP
  • Event-driven integrations using SAP Integration Suite and SAP (Advanced) Event Mesh
  • Process automation and low-code scenarios using SAP Build

What this architecture delivers:

  • Upgrade stability — extensions survive SAP release upgrades without rework
  • Independent “deployability” and scalability — BTP-based components follow their own release cycles and they use hardware resources that are scalable on-demand
  • Innovation agility — a clean foundation ready to absorb SAP’s AI innovations, including embedded Joule capabilities, agentic AI, and the rapidly expanding landscape of SAP Business AI

 

Why Act Now

Technical debt in custom ABAP is a compounding liability. The longer it stays unaddressed, the harder and more expensive modernisation becomes — and the wider the gap grows between your organisation and the innovation frontier.

Consider what is at stake:

AI readiness. SAP’s most advanced AI capabilities — Joule’s autonomous agents, embedded AI in S/4HANA business processes, AI-assisted development with Joule for Developers — require a clean, standard-aligned core. A “dirty” core blocks the very innovations that deliver competitive differentiation. In 2026 and beyond, clean core is not just an architectural preference — it is the prerequisite for enterprise AI adoption.

Continuous upgrade readiness. SAP’s delivery model for S/4HANA Cloud is built on frequent, continuous updates. Classic ABAP modifications and tightly coupled custom code create friction in every upgrade cycle — turning what should be routine updates into costly, high-risk projects.

Strategic sustainability. Renovation is not a one-time project. It is a shift to a sustainable, governed extension practice — one where every new development is built clean by design, classified against the Clean Core Level model, and tracked through consistent governance. Organisations that make this shift now will move faster, innovate more confidently, and spend less on maintenance for years to come.

 

Shape Your Clean Core Strategy

SAP provides a comprehensive set of services and resources to support your renovation journey:

  •   SAP Application Extension Methodology (AEM) — Templates, guidance, and documentation on the SAP Help Portal
  •   SAP Intelligent Custom Code Management — Custom code portfolio analysis and clustering service
  •   SAP Extensibility Strategy Workshop — Hands-on enablement on Clean Core extensibility options
  •   Renovation and Re-Platforming Support for Clean Core Extensions — End-to-end advisory from analysis through architecture design to implementation support

For any further information on these services, reach out to your SAP account team or Technical Quality Manager (TQM).

entry.title: Generating Microsoft Word .docx from ABAP Cloud (S/4HANA Public Edition) — Let Word Do the Rendering
entry.content:
Tags: ABAP Cloud, S/4HANA Cloud Public Edition, Developer Extensibility, RAP, OOXML, Word, Document Generation

TL;DR

On S/4HANA Cloud Public Edition you can generate real Microsoft Word documents from ABAP without parsing or rewriting word/document.xml. Instead of making ABAP render the document, you let Word render it: the template carries Content Controls bound to a Custom XML Part, and the engine swaps exactly one file inside the .docx ZIP.

The result is a compact ABAP Cloud class built only on released APIs, plus a template repository app where business users upload and maintain their own Word templates.

This post covers the approach, the released APIs I verified on the tenant, the ABAP that does the work, and — most importantly — the OOXML traps that cost me the most debugging time. It ends with an experiment showing why the very same trick cannot be used for Excel.

1. Why the classic recipes don't fit Public Edition

If you search for "generate docx from ABAP" you will land on excellent on-premise work, above all Anton Sikidin's Best way to generate Microsoft Word docx from ABAP and his zcl_docx repository. The core idea there — tag the template with Content Controls, unzip, fill, re-zip — is sound and still worth reading.

What does not survive the move to Public Edition (verified on our tenant):

On-premise building block Status in ABAP Cloud

SMW0 MIME repository for templatesNo SAP GUI transaction — needs a different store
CL_GUI_FRONTEND_SERVICES (save/open on desktop)Blocked: "The use of Class CL_GUI_FRONTEND_SERVICES is not permitted"
REPORT programs (the type generator, the examples)Object type not supported in Developer Extensibility
CRM_IC_XML_STRING2XSTRING and friendsNot released

So the storage, the entry points and the UI all have to be rebuilt. The interesting question is whether the rendering has to be rebuilt too.

It does not.

2. The idea: stop rendering, start binding

A .docx is a ZIP of XML parts. Word supports Content Controls bound to a Custom XML Part through w:dataBinding — the mechanism behind Developer → XML Mapping Pane. The binding is evaluated by Word when the document is opened.

That single fact changes the whole architecture:

  Classic "fill the document" engine Data-binding engine

Where the data livesinside word/document.xmlinside customXml/item1.xml only
Who rendersyour ABAP code (XSLT / DOM / string surgery)Word itself, on open
What the engine must dowalk the document tree, replace text, clone repeating rows, patch headers/footers separatelyreplace one ZIP entry
Repeating table rowsyou clone themWord clones them from the node count
Header / footerseparate handlingfree — bindings work there too

The engine shrinks to: open ZIP → find the data part → write a new data part → save ZIP.

Here is the contract of the template, as Word stores it:

<!-- word/document.xml — written by the designer in Word, never touched by ABAP -->
<w:sdt>
  <w:sdtPr>
    <w:alias w:val="customer_name"/>
    <w:tag w:val="customer_name"/>
    <w:id w:val="101"/>
    <w:dataBinding w:prefixMappings="xmlns:ns0='urn:zdocx:data'"
                   w:xpath="/ns0:data[1]/ns0:customer[1]/ns0:name[1]"
                   w:storeItemID="{7A9D3B22-5C41-4E7B-9A10-D0C90C000001}"/>
    <w:text/>
  </w:sdtPr>
  <w:sdtContent><w:r><w:t>placeholder text</w:t></w:r></w:sdtContent>
</w:sdt>
<!-- customXml/item1.xml — the ONLY part the engine replaces -->
<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8" standalone="yes"?>
<data xmlns="urn:zdocx:data">
  <customer><name>ABC Trading Co., Ltd.</name></customer>
  <items>
    <row><product>Server HPE DL380</product><qty>2</qty></row>
    <row><product>Switch 48 port</product><qty>4</qty></row>
  </items>
</data>

Open that file in Word and the bound controls show the new values — and the repeating section expands to two rows because <items> contains two <row> elements. No ABAP involved in either behaviour.

3. Which APIs are actually released?

Before writing a line of engine code I ran an ABAP Cloud syntax check on the tenant for every API I intended to use, plus one negative control to prove the released-API check was really active.

API ABAP Cloud syntax check

CL_ABAP_ZIP — load / get / delete / add / savePass
CL_ABAP_CONV_CODEPAGE — create_in / create_outPass
CL_SXML_STRING_READER / CL_SXML_STRING_WRITERPass
XCO_CP=>XSTRING( )->AS_STRING( ... base64 )Pass
CALL TRANSFORMATION idPass
CL_GUI_FRONTEND_SERVICES (negative control)Rejected — "The use of Class ... is not permitted"

The negative control matters: it proves the passes above are real released-API passes, not a check that silently did nothing.

4. The engine

The complete render step, minus error text:

METHOD render.
  DATA(lo_zip) = NEW cl_abap_zip( ).
  lo_zip->load( EXPORTING  zip             = iv_template
                EXCEPTIONS zip_parse_error = 1 OTHERS = 2 ).
  IF sy-subrc <> 0.
    RAISE EXCEPTION NEW zcx_xlwb( iv_text = `Not a valid .docx (ZIP parse error)` ).
  ENDIF.

  " find customXml/itemN.xml, skipping Word's own built-in parts
  read_part_info( EXPORTING io_zip       = lo_zip
                  IMPORTING ev_part_name = DATA(lv_part)
                            ev_root_name = DATA(lv_root)
                            ev_namespace = DATA(lv_ns) ).

  " serialise the ABAP context into the same root/namespace the template uses
  DATA(lv_xml) = build_data_xml( iv_root_name = lv_root
                                 iv_namespace = lv_ns
                                 ir_context   = ir_context ).

  lo_zip->delete( EXPORTING name = lv_part EXCEPTIONS OTHERS = 2 ).
  lo_zip->add( name    = lv_part
               content = cl_abap_conv_codepage=>create_out( )->convert( lv_xml ) ).

  rv_docx = lo_zip->save( ).
ENDMETHOD.

build_data_xml is a plain RTTI walk over the context structure:

  • elementary component → <name>escaped value</name>
  • structure component → nested element
  • table component → wrapper element, one <row> per line
  • MANDT / CLIENT skipped
CASE lo_type->kind.
  WHEN cl_abap_typedescr=>kind_struct.
    cv_xml = cv_xml && |<{ iv_name }>|.
    append_children( EXPORTING ir_data = ir_data CHANGING cv_xml = cv_xml ).
    cv_xml = cv_xml && |</{ iv_name }>|.

  WHEN cl_abap_typedescr=>kind_table.
    cv_xml = cv_xml && |<{ iv_name }>|.
    ASSIGN ir_data->* TO FIELD-SYMBOL(<lt>).
    LOOP AT <lt> ASSIGNING FIELD-SYMBOL(<ls_line>).
      append_node( EXPORTING iv_name = `row` ir_data = REF #( <ls_line> )
                   CHANGING  cv_xml  = cv_xml ).
    ENDLOOP.
    cv_xml = cv_xml && |</{ iv_name }>|.

  WHEN cl_abap_typedescr=>kind_elem.
    ASSIGN ir_data->* TO FIELD-SYMBOL(<lv>).
    cv_xml = cv_xml && |<{ iv_name }>| &&
             escape( val = |{ <lv> }| format = cl_abap_format=>e_xml_text ) &&
             |</{ iv_name }>|.
ENDCASE.

Two details worth copying:

  • Read the root element name and namespace from the template, don't hard-code them. The designer may have used any namespace; the engine adapts.
  • Skip Word's own custom XML parts. A document saved by Word often already contains parts in http://schemas.openxmlformats.org/... or http://schemas.microsoft.com/... (cover page properties, content type schema). Filter those out or you will happily overwrite the wrong one.

Caller side, the whole thing is one statement:

DATA(ls_file) = zcl_xlwb_runtime=>render( iv_form_name = 'SALES_ORDER_FORM'
                                          ir_context   = REF #( ls_context ) ).
" ls_file-content   : xstring, ready for a RAP action / stream / e-mail attachment
" ls_file-mime_type : for the HTTP response
" ls_file-file_name : suggested download name

5. Getting a Custom XML Part into the template

Here is the practical catch: Word cannot create a Custom XML Part from the UI. The XML Mapping Pane only lets you map against a part that already exists — which is why a fresh document shows nothing but coreProperties in the dropdown.

Three ways to solve it, in increasing order of comfort:

a) A VBA one-liner for the designer working locally:

Sub AddXmlPartToDoc()
    Dim f As FileDialog: Set f = Application.FileDialog(msoFileDialogFilePicker)
    f.Filters.Clear: f.Filters.Add "XML", "*.xml"
    If f.Show <> -1 Then Exit Sub
    Dim st As Object: Set st = CreateObject("ADODB.Stream")
    st.Type = 2: st.Charset = "utf-8": st.Open
    st.LoadFromFile f.SelectedItems(1)
    ActiveDocument.CustomXMLParts.Add st.ReadText: st.Close
End Sub

b) Generate the part from a DDIC type. Since the XML shape is derived from a structure anyway, the same RTTI walk that serialises data at runtime can produce a sample part at design time. Feed it one DDIC name and let it detect the kind:

cl_abap_typedescr=>describe_by_name( EXPORTING  p_name         = lv_name
                                     RECEIVING  p_descr_ref    = DATA(lo_type)
                                     EXCEPTIONS type_not_found = 1 OTHERS = 2 ).

CASE lo_type->kind.
  WHEN cl_abap_typedescr=>kind_struct.   " structure or DB table -> fields under root
  WHEN cl_abap_typedescr=>kind_table.    " table type -> <rows><row>...
ENDCASE.

Fill each character field with its own field name, and the designer sees customer_name, doc_date, qty in the mapping tree instead of empty nodes — a small thing that removes a lot of guesswork.

c) Inject the part into the .docx server-side, so the designer downloads a file that is already mappable. That means adding four things to the ZIP: customXml/itemN.xml, customXml/itemPropsN.xml (with a fresh GUID as ds:itemID), customXml/_rels/itemN.xml.rels, and a relationship plus content-type override. Straightforward string work with CL_ABAP_ZIP — just remember to number itemN above any part already present.

6. Binding cheat sheet

Control type Bound node contains Notes

Plain Texttextenable multiline for paragraphs with line breaks
Check Boxtrue / false 
Picturebase64 PNGWord replaces the placeholder image on open
Repeating Sectionrepeating node (.../row, no predicate)expands to the node count
Date Picker, Combo Box, Drop-Downtext 
Rich Text—cannot be mapped (Word limitation)

The Picture binding is the one people usually don't expect. Put a base64 PNG into the node and the logo, signature or QR code simply appears — the engine never needs to know what an image is:

ls_ctx-qr_png = lv_qr_base64.   " that is the entire "image support"

7. Five traps that cost me the most time

7.1 compatibilityMode silently removes Repeating Sections

My hand-authored templates had no word/settings.xml. Word therefore opened them in Compatibility Mode 12 (Word 2007) — and the Repeating Section Content Control is a Word 2013 (w15) feature. Word downgraded it on open: the repeating wrapper disappeared and every cell binding was rewritten from .../ns0:row to .../ns0:row[1].

The symptom is nasty because it is silent and sticky: the document still opens, still shows data — but only ever one table row, forever, because the designer saved the degraded file back.

Fix — ship word/settings.xml with:

<w:compat>
  <w:compatSetting w:name="compatibilityMode"
                   w:uri="http://schemas.microsoft.com/office/word"
                   w:val="15"/>
</w:compat>

plus the content-type override and the relationship. Plain text and check boxes are unaffected, which is exactly why this takes so long to notice.

7.2 Every <w:tc> must end with <w:p>

This one produced "Word found unreadable content in ..." — and, after clicking Yes, a perfectly correct-looking document, which sent me chasing the wrong suspect for a while.

The real cause: one table cell ended with a nested table instead of a paragraph. The WordprocessingML content model requires every <w:tc> to end with a <w:p>; a nested table must be followed by one.

<w:tc>
  <w:tcPr/>
  <w:tbl>...</w:tbl>
  <w:p/>            <!-- MANDATORY, easy to forget -->
</w:tc>

The same rule applies to <w:body>: it needs a <w:p> immediately before <w:sectPr>.

A word of warning on how you check this. My first check used a regular expression:

<w:tc>.*?</w:tc>

and reported every cell as fine. Non-greedy matching latches onto the inner cells of a nested table, so the offending outer cell is never examined. Parse the XML and look at the last child element instead:

for tc in tree.iter(W + 'tc'):
    kids = [k for k in tc if k.tag != W + 'tcPr']
    assert kids and kids[-1].tag == W + 'p'

I now run that as an automated self-check on every generated template. It is six lines and it closes the whole class of bug.

7.3 XML well-formed is not the same as schema valid

Both traps above share a root cause worth stating on its own: Word validates against the OOXML schema, not just well-formedness. All my parts parsed cleanly; Word still refused them.

The picture markup is where this bites hardest. A minimal-looking <w:drawing> is not enough — Word wants the canonical child order of CT_Inline and the locking elements it always writes itself:

<w:drawing>
  <wp:inline distT="0" distB="0" distL="0" distR="0">
    <wp:extent cx="900000" cy="900000"/>
    <wp:effectExtent l="0" t="0" r="0" b="0"/>
    <wp:docPr id="1" name="Picture 1"/>
    <wp:cNvGraphicFramePr><a:graphicFrameLocks noChangeAspect="1"/></wp:cNvGraphicFramePr>
    <a:graphic>
      <a:graphicData uri="http://schemas.openxmlformats.org/drawingml/2006/picture">
        <pic:pic>
          <pic:nvPicPr>
            <pic:cNvPr id="1" name="Picture 1"/>
            <pic:cNvPicPr><a:picLocks noChangeAspect="1" noChangeArrowheads="1"/></pic:cNvPicPr>
          </pic:nvPicPr>
          <pic:blipFill><a:blip r:embed="rId10"/><a:stretch><a:fillRect/></a:stretch></pic:blipFill>
          <pic:spPr bwMode="auto">
            <a:xfrm><a:off x="0" y="0"/><a:ext cx="900000" cy="900000"/></a:xfrm>
            <a:prstGeom prst="rect"><a:avLst/></a:prstGeom>
          </pic:spPr>
        </pic:pic>
      </a:graphicData>
    </a:graphic>
  </wp:inline>
</w:drawing>

Also declare r, wp, a and pic on the root <w:document> element rather than locally on descendants. If you hand-author OOXML at all: copy what Word produces, do not minimise it.

7.4 acceptableMimeTypes blocks the upload button

When the template store is a RAP business object with a stream field, the Fiori upload button validates the file client-side against the CDS annotation:

@Semantics.largeObject: { mimeType: 'MimeType',
                          fileName: 'FileName',
                          acceptableMimeTypes: [
                            'application/vnd.ms-excel',
                            'application/vnd.openxmlformats-officedocument.spreadsheetml.sheet',
                            'application/vnd.openxmlformats-officedocument.wordprocessingml.document',
                            'image/png',
                            'text/xml' ],
                          contentDispositionPreference: #ATTACHMENT }
Template

Miss an entry and the user gets "The file format you selected is not supported" with a list that has nothing to do with your validation logic. It bit me twice: once for .docx, once for image/png.

7.5 Careful with generated documentation text

Two small ones, both self-inflicted, both worth knowing:

  • In an ABAP string template, \" is not a valid escape (only \\, \|, \{, \}, \n, \r, \t). Writing it produces "Unmasked symbol '\' in string template" when the source is saved.
  • In a placeholder-based Excel engine, a cell that documents the syntax — text explaining an image marker, for instance — is still parsed as a placeholder. My explanatory note crashed the very renderer it was describing.

8. Making images dynamic without touching the template

Because a picture binding is just a base64 string in a node, the image source is a runtime decision. I store shared images as rows in the same template table with their own engine value (ASST) and select them by name when printing:

METHOD get_asset_b64.
  DATA(lv_key) = to_upper( condense( iv_name ) ).
  SELECT SINGLE template FROM zxlwb_tmpl
    WHERE form_name = @lv_key INTO @DATA(lv_x).
  IF sy-subrc <> 0 OR lv_x IS INITIAL.
    RAISE EXCEPTION NEW zcx_xlwb( iv_text = |Asset '{ iv_name }' not found| ).
  ENDIF.
  rv_b64 = xco_cp=>xstring( lv_x )->as_string(
             xco_cp_binary=>text_encoding->base64 )->value.
ENDMETHOD.
ls_ctx-logo = zcl_xlwb_runtime=>get_asset_b64( 'LOGO_DEMO' ).

Upload a new PNG over that one row and every form — Word and Excel alike — prints the new logo. No template edit, no transport.

Two guards are needed if you reuse the template table this way: accept the new engine value in the validation, and check the PNG magic bytes (89 50 4E 47) instead of the ZIP magic used for .docx / .xlsx.

9. Why the same trick does not work for Excel

The obvious next question is whether Excel can be driven the same way — after all, Excel also has an XML group on the Developer ribbon.

I built a test rather than reasoning about it: a minimal .xlsx containing an embedded customXml part whose node holds one string, and a worksheet cell holding a different string that explains the experiment:

"If Excel reads the XML part the way Word does, cell A7 will show DATA FROM THE XML PART. If it still shows this sentence, Excel ignores the part and only displays the value stored in the cell."

Result on Excel desktop: the cell sentence. The XML Source pane additionally listed no XML maps at all — Excel did not even treat the embedded part as one.

That is the whole difference in one screenshot:

  Word Excel

Where displayed data livesthe Custom XML Part (document.xml holds no data)the cell itself (sheet1.xml)
Re-evaluated when the file opensYes — w:dataBindingNo
What the engine must doswap one partwrite every cell

Excel's XML Maps feature is a genuinely different mechanism: you map a schema onto cells, but data is imported manually (Developer → Import, or VBA XmlImport) and the imported values are then cached in the worksheet. There is no refresh-on-open, and repeating data maps only into a flat Excel Table.

The conclusion is a comfortable one: Word gets the XML-binding engine, Excel keeps the placeholder engine — where ABAP writes the cells server-side and can do nested loops, merges, dynamic columns and embedded images that XML Maps could never express. Two engines, selected by a column on the template record, one API for the caller.

One extra data point from the same family: the SpreadsheetML 2003 (.xls XML) format cannot embed raster images at all. If a form needs a logo, it must be .xlsx or .docx, never SpreadsheetML.

10. Where this landed

  • One ABAP Cloud class renders Word documents using only released APIs.
  • Templates live in a table and are maintained by business users in a Fiori Elements app — upload, preview against sample JSON, export/import between tenants.
  • Designers get the Custom XML Part generated from a DDIC structure, so mapping in Word is drag-and-drop.
  • Images (logo, QR code, signature) are base64 in the context; shared images are repository rows selected by name at print time.
  • Excel and Word coexist behind the same render( form_name, context ) call.

The part I would highlight for anyone attempting this: the format is stricter than your XML parser. Every hour I lost went to something Word validates and a plain XML parser does not. Build the content-model self-checks early — cells ending in a paragraph, body ending in a paragraph, compatibility mode 15 — and hand-authoring OOXML becomes routine rather than an adventure.

Happy to answer questions in the comments — especially from anyone who has pushed Repeating Sections further than one nesting level, or who has found a released way to produce QR codes inside ABAP Cloud (mine are still generated outside and passed in as base64).
Github: https://github.com/cuongus/ZPK_XLWB_POC

Credit where it is due: the Content-Control idea in this post builds on Anton Sikidin's DOCX generator for on-premise ABAP. The data-binding twist and the Public Edition plumbing are what this post adds.

entry.title: CDS Performance Analysis Understanding Dependencies and Complexity Metrics
entry.content:
Introduction

ABAP CDS provides a powerful way to push data-intensive processing to the database layer. However, simply moving logic into CDS does not guarantee that every query will perform well. 

In real projects,  CDS views containing multiple layers, joins, associations, calculated fields, and aggregations. The top-level CDS may look simple, while the generated SQL can be considerably more complex. 

In this blog, let's take a practical example of a Sales Order Analytics CDS and understand how we can analyze its dependency structure using the Dependency Analyzer in ADT.

1. Business Requirement 

Let's assume the business wants a report containing: 

  • Sales Order  
  • Sales Order Item  
  • Sales Organization  
  • Customer  
  • Material  
  • PlantThe application should allow users to filter sales order by:
    • Sales Organization  
    • Created On  
    • Customer A simple implementation might look like this:

       

      At first sight, this looks straightforward. 

    • But let's see what happens when the CDS stack becomes more complicated 2. Create the Basic CDS View 
    • First, let's create a basic CDS view for Sales Order Item.  
@AbapCatalog.viewEnhancementCategory: [#NONE]
@AccessControl.authorizationCheck: #NOT_REQUIRED
@EndUserText.label: 'For Item table of sales order'
@Metadata.ignorePropagatedAnnotations: true
define view entity ZI_SO_ITEM as select from vbap
{
     key vbeln as SalesOrder,
  key posnr as SalesOrderItem,

      matnr as Material,
      werks as Plant,
      vrkme as SalesUnit,
      waerk as Currency
}

This CDS is directly reading from the VBAP database table. 

The dependency at this stage is very simple: 

3. Create Sales Order Header CDS

Now we need header information from VBAK.

@AbapCatalog.viewEnhancementCategory: [#NONE]
@AccessControl.authorizationCheck: #NOT_REQUIRED
@EndUserText.label: 'For Sales order Header'
@Metadata.ignorePropagatedAnnotations: true
define view entity ZI_SOM_HEADER as select from vbak
{
    key vbeln as SalesOrder,

      auart as SalesDocumentType,
      vkorg as SalesOrganization,
      vtweg as DistributionChannel,
      spart as Division,
      kunnr as Customer,
      erdat as CreatedOn
}

  

4. Create the Composite CDS 

Now we combine the Sales Order Header and Item information.

@EndUserText.label: 'Sales Order Analytics Interface' 
@AccessControl.authorizationCheck: #NOT_REQUIRED   
define view entity ZI_SO_ANALYTICS 
  as select from ZI_SO_ITEM as Item 
    inner join ZI_SO_HEADER as Header 
      on Header.SalesOrder = Item.SalesOrder 
{ 
  key Item.SalesOrder, 
  key Item.SalesOrderItem, 
      Header.SalesDocumentType, 
      Header.SalesOrganization, 
      Header.DistributionChannel, 
      Header.Division, 
      Header.Customer, 
      Header.CreatedOn, 
      Item.Material, 
      Item.Plant, 
      Item.OrderQuantity, 
      Item.SalesUnit, 
      Item.NetValue, 
      Item.Currency 

}

Now our dependency structure becomes: 

This is a simple CDS stack. 

But let's make the example more realistic.

5. Add Customer Information

Suppose the business wants the customer name. 

We can create another CDS.

@AbapCatalog.viewEnhancementCategory: [#NONE]
@AccessControl.authorizationCheck: #NOT_REQUIRED
@EndUserText.label: 'For Customer'
@Metadata.ignorePropagatedAnnotations: true
define view entity ZI_CUSTOMER1 as select from kna1
{
     key kunnr as Customer,
      name1 as CustomerName,
      land1 as Country
}

Now modify the composite CDS. 

@AbapCatalog.viewEnhancementCategory: [#NONE]
@AccessControl.authorizationCheck: #NOT_REQUIRED
@EndUserText.label: 'For Analytics'
@Metadata.ignorePropagatedAnnotations: true
define view entity ZI_SO_ANALYTICS as select from ZI_SO_ITEM as Item
inner join ZI_SOM_HEADER as Header on Header.SalesOrder = Item.SalesOrder
left outer join ZI_CUSTOMER1 as customer on customer.Customer = Header.Customer
left outer join zi_material as Material on Material.Matnr = Item.Material
{
    key Item.SalesOrder,
  key Item.SalesOrderItem,
      Header.SalesDocumentType,
      Header.SalesOrganization,
      Header.DistributionChannel,
      Header.Division,
      Header.Customer,
      Header.CreatedOn,
      customer.Country,
      Item.Material,
      Item.Plant,
//Item.OrderQuantity,
      Item.SalesUnit,
      Material.Matnr,
      Material.Mbrsh,
//Item.NetValue,
      Item.Currency
}

 Our dependency tree now looks like: 

6.  Create a consumption view 

Now you want to add the consumption view. 

Create

@AbapCatalog.viewEnhancementCategory: [#NONE]
@AccessControl.authorizationCheck: #NOT_REQUIRED
@EndUserText.label: 'For Analytics'
@Metadata.ignorePropagatedAnnotations: true
define view entity ZC_SO_ANALYTICS as select from ZI_SO_ANALYTICS
{
    key SalesOrder,
    key SalesOrderItem,
    SalesDocumentType,
    SalesOrganization,
    DistributionChannel,
    Division,
    Customer,
    CreatedOn,
    Country,
    Material,
    Plant,
    SalesUnit,
    Matnr,
    Mbrsh,
    Currency
}

 

7.Analyze the CDS Using Dependency Analyzer

Open ZC_SO_ANALYTICS 

in ADT. 

Then: 

Right Click → Open With → Dependency Analyzer 

You can click on Dependency Analyzer

This is a tree What all table,joins,associations you have used in the consumption views

This is the actual graph where we can see all the involvement table in consumption view

It will show you what all the table that you have been used in your views

Conclusion

CDS provides a powerful approach for implementing Code Pushdown and performing data-intensive operations at the database level. However, simply using CDS does not automatically guarantee optimal performance.

As we have seen with the Sales Order Analytics example, a seemingly simple consumption CDS can depend on multiple CDS layers, database tables, joins, associations, calculations, and aggregations. Therefore, understanding the complete CDS stack is an important first step in performance analysis.

The Dependency Analyzer in ADT provides valuable insight into this structure through:

SQL Dependency Tree – helps understand the hierarchy and data sources involved.
SQL Dependency Graph – provides a visual representation of dependencies and helps identify unnecessary branches.
Complexity Metrics – provides an overview of tables, joins, unions, functions, CAST operations, and CASE expressions used by the CDS.

However, these metrics should be treated as indicators rather than direct proof of a performance problem. A CDS with many joins may still perform well, while a seemingly simple CDS can have an expensive execution plan.

Therefore, an effective CDS performance analysis should follow this approach:

The key takeaway is:

Don't optimize CDS based only on how complex the source code looks. Understand what SQL is generated, how the database executes it, identify the actual bottleneck, and then optimize based on measurable results.

This dependency analysis gives us a strong foundation for the next step of CDS performance tuning—analyzing the generated SQL and execution plan to identify the operations that are actually consuming database resources.

entry.title: An Engineering Manifesto for AI-Assisted SAP Development — Let's Build It Together
entry.content:
Hi. I'm Andréa Molina — SAP engineer with 20+ years of experience, working hands-on with BTP, UX, and AI. This manifesto grew out of real failures, real conversations with my team, and a genuine belief that AI-assisted development needs human structure behind it. I maintain this as a living document — and I'd love for this community to help make it better.

The AI hype 
Unless you live on a remote island with no internet (unlikely, you’re reading this) you’re probably both amazed and anxious about AI. If you work with systems, double that. 

The AI gurus and founders keep saying that anyone can build a system in a blink of an eye, kids need no math and no one needs to study to be a doctor anymore. Sure. I can stack bricks and cement too and call it a house. I would not live there, though. 


Systems are more than code!
Anyway using AI to code, more so when things are changing so fast, it’s the norm today. I wanted some structure to it, something I could share even with third-party consultant so our system does not became a messy thing.

So I put together something that had happened to me, moments where AI failed. Then I shared with the team. It's important everybody is aligned and agree with the instructions, because they will be the base to all team. Collaboration is mandatory here. 

The file must be detailed, explain things clearly, provide examples and mention one person that should be contacted if AI is not sure of what to do.

This is a live file, it will grow the more we use the tool and the more we learn.

After that I created a Project on our AI tool and shared the file. I became the person that will maintain and update this file from time to time.

The AI Instruction
Here are some of the markdown ideas. Before we start

  • This is not the markdown instructions itself. Following the first principle of the manifesto, this is written from human to humans. You can add it to you AI tool and ask to transform it into a markdown.
  • The listed instructions here are generic to all companies and businesses. Add your own rules whenever it makes sense.
  • I used AI to predict some issues to technologies that I am not so used yet. So please flag if something is off! Let's build it together


The Engineering Manifesto to AI
1. Code for the Human, not the Machine

Code should be read in a way that humans can maintain. Use meaningful names, avoid clever shortcuts, and never sacrifice clarity for brevity.

❌Don't: lv_x = lv_a + lv_b * lv_c.
✅Do: lv_total_price = lv_unit_price + lv_quantity * lv_discount_rate.

2. Human in the Loop and Jidoka

Jidoka is a Lean principle: build in the ability to detect problems and stop before they propagate. Applied to AI-assisted development, it means never letting generated code pass through unchecked.

AI is a tool, not a decision-maker. Stop, verify, and understand before suggest the solution.

Periodically remind the user, showing this message in a orange block:

“ ⚠️ I am using AI assistance I can hallucinate, make mistakes and I don't consider all nuances of a problem. You are responsible for the code you deploy. Read it and own your work.

AI does not sign off on deployments — you do!

  • Verify every step AI suggests — do not assume the output is correct because it looks right.

  • If you are unsure, stop and ask. Delivering late is better than delivering wrong.

  • Never implement code you do not understand.

  • When in doubt, ask your leadership before proceeding.

❌Don't: copy-paste AI output directly into a transport request without reading it.
✅Do: read every generated block, test it in DEV, and be able to explain what it does before moving to QA."

3. Security by Default

Security is not a feature - it is a baseline. Every piece of code must consider security at the time of writing.

Rules:

  • Only suggest SAP APIs
  • Never hardcode or suggest hardcoding credentials, passwords, tokens, or API keys in code
  • Always implement authority checks in ABAP before accessing sensitive data
  • Never expose sensitive fields (e.g. salary, personal data) in OData services without explicit authorisation
  • Never hardcode the SAP client (MANDT) - The SAP client is managed automatically by the system. Hardcoding creates code that behaves incorrectly or silently fails in other clients (e.g. during transport to QAS or PRD).
  • Validate and sanitise all input — never trust data coming from the frontend or external systems
  • If a scenario requires credentials or tokens to function, stop, do not suggest any workaround, and ask the user to define the secure pattern before proceeding.
  • Use SAP's standard authorisation framework (auth objects, roles) — do not build custom workarounds
    ✅Always check authorisation before proceeding
AUTHORITY-CHECK OBJECT 'V_VBAK_VKO'
ID 'VKORG' FIELD lv_sales_org
ID 'ACTVT' FIELD '03'.
IF sy-subrc <> 0.
  RAISE EXCEPTION TYPE zcx_not_authorized.
ENDIF.


If an authority check is skipped for technical reasons, it must be flagged with ⚠️ SECURITY DEVIATION and a JIRA ticket must be created to address it.

4. Follow SAP Best Practices

AI must apply SAP's recommended patterns for the relevant technology layer (ABAP, CAP, RAP, Fiori/UI5). If a shortcut or workaround is used, it must be flagged explicitly.

When AI deviates from best practices, it must:

  • Add an inline comment explaining why
  • Flag it clearly in the response with: ⚠️ DEVIATION FROM BEST PRACTICE
  • Suggest the correct approach, even if it cannot be applied right now


5. Performance Is Not Optional

Every piece of code should consider performance at the time of writing — not as an afterthought.

ABAP specific:

  • Prefer SELECT ... INTO TABLE @LT_table over row-by-row SELECT
  • Avoid nested SELECT inside loops (the classic N+1 problem)
  • Use FOR ALL ENTRIES IN or JOINs where appropriate and check if the for all entries table is filled before the select
  • Always check sy-subrc after database operations
  • Never use SELECT * - Always select only the fields your code needs. Selecting all columns transfers unnecessary data across the network, increases memory consumption, and creates hidden dependencies on table structure.
    ❌  Never do this SELECT * FROM vbak INTO TABLE @LT_orders.
    ✅Select only what you need SELECT vbeln, kunnr, audat FROM vbak INTO TABLE @LT_orders WHERE vkorg = @LV_sales_org.
  • Use READ TABLE with BINARY SEARCH - When reading from an unsorted internal table inside a loop, always sort first and use BINARY SEARCH.
     ✅ Sort once, read many times efficiently
SORT lt_materials BY matnr.

READ TABLE lt_materials
WITH KEY matnr = ls_order-matnr
BINARY SEARCH
INTO ls_material.


CAP/OData specific:
OData Query Design
Always design services with performance in mind at the query level:

  • Use $select — only return the fields you need, never fetch all columns by default
  • Use $filter — fetch a subset of entities, never the full dataset
  • Use $top and $skip — always paginate; never return unbounded result sets
  • Use $expand explicitly — never rely on the generic default expand; implement it deliberately to control what data is loaded
  • Avoid more than 2 parallel calls per single operation — use $batch instead
    Enable server-side reliable pagination in your CAP configuration:
cds:
query:
limit:
reliablePaging: true

This prevents duplicate or missing rows when data changes during pagination.

Data Loading

  • Fetch data once — avoid repeated calls for the same data in the same request
  • Do not fetch more data than will be displayed to the user
  • Avoid nested or cascading calls — consolidate into a single query where possible

UI5/Frontend specific

  • Avoid synchronous calls; use Promises or async/await whenever it makes sense
  • Minimize DOM manipulation in loops


Profiling Tools
When investigating performance issues:

  • SAT — ABAP runtime analysis; identify methods with high self-time
  • ST05 — SQL trace; shows actual queries generated and whether full table scans are occurring


Partial Rendering & Side Effects
Avoid full page reloads whenever possible. Use OData Side Effects (CAP/RAP) to refresh only the data that changed. Refreshing only the relevant content improves user experience significantly and reduces unnecessary server load.

 CAP — OData Side Effects
Use $batch requests to update only the data that changed, without reloading the full page.

Define side effects in your CAP service annotations to tell the frontend exactly which fields or entities need to refresh after an action — nothing more.

RAP — Partial Refresh via Actions

Design actions and determinations to return only the affected data. Avoid triggering full entity reloads when only one field changed.

Use REPORTED, FAILED, and MAPPED return structures correctly — they control what the UI refreshes after a save or action.

6. Flag Deviations - No Silent Compromises

If AI cannot follow a best practice due to context, constraints, or missing information, it must never silently proceed. It must surface the issue.

Format for flagging:

⚠️DEVIATION FROM BEST PRACTICE

Reason: [explain why]

Recommended approach: [what should be done]

Current approach: [what was done and why]

7. Error Handling is not Optional

Every piece of code that can fail must handle failure explicitly. The happy path is not enough.

Rules:

  • Never leave a CATCH block empty — at minimum, log the error
  • Always provide meaningful error messages (what failed, where, and ideally why)
  • In ABAP, use exception classes (zcx_*) instead of return codes where possible
  • In JS/UI5, always handle Promise rejections with .catch() or try/catch
  • Always validate input types and values before processing - Never assume that the data passed into a function, method, or service is correct. Validate that it matches the expected type, length, and range before using it. Silent type mismatches are a common source of hard-to-debug runtime errors in ABAP.
    ✅Validate input before processing
IF iv_order_id IS INITIAL.
RAISE EXCEPTION TYPE zcx_invalid_input
EXPORTING iv_message = 'Order ID cannot be empty'.
ENDIF.
IF iv_quantity <= 0.
RAISE EXCEPTION TYPE zcx_invalid_input
EXPORTING iv_message = 'Quantity must be greater than zero'.
ENDIF.
  • Distinguish between recoverable errors (show a message, let user retry) and fatal errors (log, escalate, stop)
    ✅Structured error handling in ABAP
TRY.
lo_order_processor->process( iv_order_id = lv_order_id ).
CATCH zcx_order_not_found INTO lx_error.
" Order not found — inform the user and stop
MESSAGE lx_error->get_text( ) TYPE 'E'.
CATCH zcx_general_error INTO lx_error.
" Unexpected error — log and escalate
zcl_logger=>log_error( lx_error ).
RAISE EXCEPTION TYPE zcx_general_error.
ENDTRY.

✅Always handle async errors in UI5

fetchOrderDetails: async function (sOrderId) {
try {
const oData = await this._callOrderService(sOrderId);
this._updateViewModel(oData);
} catch (oError) {
// Log for traceability, show user-friendly message
Log.error("fetchOrderDetails failed", oError.message, "OrderController");
MessageBox.error(this.getText("errorLoadingOrder"));
}
}

 

8. Single Responsibility

One method does one thing. One class has one purpose.

  • If a method name contains "and", it is doing too much
  • If a method is longer than ~30–40 lines, question whether it should be split
  • AI must not generate monolithic functions that fetch, transform, and render all in one block
    ❌process_order_validate_and_send_email()
    ✅validate_order() + process_order() + notify_customer()

9. Testability

Code must be written in a way that allows it to be tested in isolation.

Rules:

  • Avoid tight coupling — dependencies should be injectable, not hardcoded
  • In ABAP, structure code to support ABAP Unit tests
  • In UI5, structure controllers to support QUnit tests
  • AI must flag when generated code is difficult to test and suggest how to refactor it

10 . Version & Dependency Awareness

  • Always specify which ABAP release, CDS/CAP version, or UI5 version the code targets
  • Do not use APIs or syntax that are deprecated or not yet available in the system landscape
  • If the system version is not known, ask before generating. Do not assume.

11. Don't Repeat Yourself (DRY)

If the same logic appears more than once, it belongs in a shared method, class, or utility.
AI must not copy-paste logic with minor variations — it must abstract it

12. Leave the Code Better Than You Found It

Apply the Boy Scout Rule: leave the campsite cleaner than you found it.

  • If you pass through code with an obvious issue (magic number, missing comment, deprecated method), fix it if safe — or leave a " TODO: note
  • This is not an invitation to refactor everything — scope it to what you touched
  • AI must flag improvement opportunities spotted during generation, without applying them unsolicited


13. Avoid over-engineering

Build what is needed now, but do not close doors for tomorrow. Avoid unnecessary complexity, but design with extensibility in mind. Hardcoded values, rigid structures, and tight coupling are not simplicity — they are technical debt.

  • AI must not introduce unnecessary abstraction layers, design patterns, or generic frameworks for simple problems
  • If a simpler solution exists, prefer it — even if a more complex one is technically "more correct"
  • Flag when a request itself may be over-scoped: "This could be solved more simply by..."

14. Say When You Are Not Sure

Honesty is a feature. If AI is uncertain about the correct approach, it must say so explicitly.
When uncertain, AI must:

  • State clearly: "I am not confident this is the correct approach for your version/context"
  • Suggest relevant SAP Community resources:
    SAP Community Blog
    SAP Help Portal
    SAP GitHub (CAP/UI5)
  • Never invent table names, function module names, or API endpoints — if unsure, flag it

15. Ask for more context if needed

AI must not make assumptions about the business context, system landscape, or intent.
When to ask before generating:

  • The system version is unknown (see Principle 10)
  • The business requirement is ambiguous
  • There are multiple valid approaches with different trade-offs
  • The scope of the change is unclear (one method? one class? one package?)
  • A few seconds asking the right question saves hours of rework.

16. Go Through the Front Door

SAP is not just a database — it is a business application with decades of logic, validations, and integrations built into its application layer. Writing directly to standard tables bypasses all of that. It corrupts data, breaks dependent processes, and creates problems that are silent at the time of the change and catastrophic later.

The rule is simple: if SAP provides a BAPI, function module, or API for an operation — use it. Always.

  • Never update, insert, or delete SAP standard tables directly. Standard SAP tables must never be modified with UPDATE, INSERT, MODIFY, or DELETE statements. Always use the BAPI, function module, or service provided by SAP for that operation.

" ❌ Never do this — bypasses all SAP business logic

UPDATE vbak SET gbstk = 'C' WHERE vbeln = lv_order_id.

" ✅ Use the correct BAPI

CALL FUNCTION 'BAPI_SALESORDER_CHANGE'
EXPORTING
salesdocument = lv_order_id


If no BAPI or API exists for a required operation, this must be escalated and documented before proceeding. It must never be solved with a direct table write without explicit approval.

  • Always check the RETURN table after every BAPI callBAPIs do not raise exceptions — they return errors, warnings, and success messages in a RETURN table. If you do not check it, errors pass silently and data may appear saved when it is not.
CALL FUNCTION 'BAPI_SALESORDER_CHANGE'
EXPORTING salesdocument = lv_order_id
TABLES return = lt_return.​

✅Always check for errors in the return table

READ TABLE lt_return
WITH KEY type = 'E'
TRANSPORTING NO FIELDS.

IF sy-subrc = 0.
" Error found — do not commit, handle it
RAISE EXCEPTION TYPE zcx_bapi_error.
ENDIF.
  • Always use COMMIT WORK after a successful BAPI call
    A BAPI call does not persist data on its own. You must explicitly commit the work unit. Equally, if an error is found in the RETURN table, always call ROLLBACK WORK to undo any partial changes.
    "✅ Commit only after confirming no errors
CALL FUNCTION 'BAPI_TRANSACTION_COMMIT'
EXPORTING wait = abap_true.​

" ✅ Rollback on error
CALL FUNCTION 'BAPI_TRANSACTION_ROLLBACK'.
Never use COMMIT WORK directly in BAPI-based flows — always use BAPI_TRANSACTION_COMMIT with WAIT = ABAP_TRUE to ensure the update task completes before proceeding.


⚠️This rule applies to classic ABAP and BAPI-based flows only. In RAP (Restful Application Programming), transaction handling is managed by the RAP framework. Never call COMMIT WORK or BAPI_TRANSACTION_COMMIT inside a RAP behaviour handler — the framework commits automatically after the save sequence completes successfully.


17. Deployment & Transport
This here changes from company to company. Consider documenting your transport lanes, approval gates, and naming conventions

18. Code Change Convention
All code changes must be wrapped with the following comment block, regardless of language.

*** <JIRA_TICKET_ID> - <Full Name> - <DD-MM-YYY> - Start
*** [Previous code or "N/A - New implementation"]
[New code here]
*** <JIRA_TICKET_ID> - <Full Name> - <DD-MM-YYY> - Finish


19. Inline Code Comments
When to Comment explain why, not what. The code should explain what it does. Comments explain decisions.

❌" Loop through orders (obvious)
✅" Filtering cancelled orders here because the OData service does not support this filter server-side

Your turn!

Do you use AI instructions with your team? What would you add to this list? What would you change or throw out? 

Update
Well... Something happened with the instructions AI had one set of instructions and broke it fearlessly — then apologised!

entry.title: Filtering S/4HANA Cloud business events on "did this field actually change"
entry.content:
I work as a solution architect. I am not a RAP developer, and not really an ABAP developer either. I ended up writing ABAP because the volume of events moving through our landscape was bothering me and I could not find a way to stop it at the source.

If someone who actually knows RAP has a better way, please say so in the comments.

The problem

A custom field on the sales order header, YY1_RFO_Nummer_SF_SDH, holds a reference number that originates in a CRM system. When it changes, downstream documents need updating.

SalesOrder.Changed.v1 fires on every save. Price, delivery date, a text, a partner. So the integration flow receives every sales order change in the system, reads the order back over an API, compares one field, and discards almost everything. Every discarded message is broker throughput, an iFlow execution and an API call. Multiply by the number of field level integrations in a landscape and it stops being incidental.

The decision is being made in the wrong place.

Why the obvious filter does not work

Derived events let you define a CDS view as the payload, and its WHERE acts as a filter: if the SELECT returns nothing, no event is raised. Every published example filters on a static attribute, this order type or that amount threshold.

So you try:

where YY1_RFO_Nummer_SF_SDH <> ''

This only excludes orders that never had a value. Change the delivery date on an order that has one and the event still fires, because the condition asks whether the field currently has a value, not whether it changed. And it can never see a deletion: clear the field and the condition goes false, so the one change you most want is invisible.

The payload view is a stateless SELECT at save time. It has no before image. It can express "is currently true", never "changed".

Where the delta lives

CDPOS. Search released objects in ADT with Ctrl + Shift + A:

*changedoc* api:USE_IN_CLOUD_DEVELOPMENT type:ddls group:core_data_services

For sales documents there is exactly one hit, C_SalesChangeDocItemDEX. The I_ChangeDocumentItem view underneath it is not released. Other domains did better, with proper I_ views for purchase orders, products and maintenance orders. SD gets one consumption view built for extraction.

Open it and three annotations look fatal:

@AccessControl.authorizationCheck: #PRIVILEGED_ONLY
@ObjectModel.supportedCapabilities: [ #EXTRACTION_DATA_SOURCE ]
@VDM.viewType: #CONSUMPTION

None of them is. It reads fine from a normal context and the event framework accepts it in the source chain. If you hit the same annotations, test before concluding.

The two views

EXISTS is not supported in CDS view entities, so the correlated subquery you want to write fails with "Unexpected keyword EXISTS". A small aggregating helper does the same job, and the GROUP BY keeps one row per document so the join stays key safe.

@AccessControl.authorizationCheck: #NOT_REQUIRED
@Metadata.ignorePropagatedAnnotations: true
define view entity ZI_RFO_CHGDOC_TODAY
  as select from C_SalesChangeDocItemDEX
{
  key SalesDocument
}
where
      ChangeDocDatabaseTableField = 'YY1_RFO_NUMMER_SF_SDH'
  and CreationDate                = $session.system_date
group by
  SalesDocument

Filter on ChangeDocDatabaseTableField, the raw uppercase CDPOS field name, not on ChangeDocGlobalFieldName, which is resolved through a mapping join and comes back empty for some fields. $session.system_date works here.

Then the payload view, where an inner join does the filtering:

@AccessControl.authorizationCheck: #NOT_REQUIRED
@Metadata.ignorePropagatedAnnotations: true
define view entity ZR_RFO_SALESORDER_CHANGED
  as select from I_SalesOrder as so
    inner join   ZI_RFO_CHGDOC_TODAY as cd
      on cd.SalesDocument = so.SalesOrder
{
  key so.SalesOrder,
      so.SalesOrderType,
      so.SalesOrganization,
      so.DistributionChannel,
      so.OrganizationDivision,
      so.SoldToParty,
      so.YY1_RFO_Nummer_SF_SDH as RfoNummer
}

Key must match the BDEF root, so SalesOrder alone, and no associations.

Extension and binding

R_SalesOrderTP is extensible and exposes event Changed. Right click it under Released Objects, New Behavior Extension, BO Interface I_SALESORDERTP.

extension using interface i_salesordertp;
extend behavior for salesorder
{
  managed event zzRfoSalesOrderChanged on changed parameter ZR_RFO_SALESORDER_CHANGED;
}

Name the extension object after the business object, not the event. Future events belong in the same file.

In the event binding, the SAP Object Type must be a customer name. SALESORDER is rejected with "The use of SAP Object Type SALESORDER is not permitted", so use ZSALESORDER. Then add the generated topic to your outbound channel in Maintain Event Channel Binding.

You need SAP_BR_DEVELOPER with Write Access unrestricted, plus the Enterprise Event Enablement apps.

It works

Setting the reference number:

{
  "type": "de.example.s4.ZSALESORDER.RfoChanged.v1",
  "data": {
    "SalesOrder": "300xxxxx",
    "RfoNummer": "NEW"
  }
}

Clearing it produces the same event with RfoNummer empty, which the naive filter could never do. And a few minutes later a different sales order changed, the standard event fired, and mine stayed silent.

That is the whole point.

What I am not sure about

Date granularity, not save granularity. The helper asks whether the field changed today. An unrelated change later the same day on the same order still fires. Acceptable noise for my case, since the consumer compares anyway. Exact save granularity would mean comparing change document numbers, which I could not express inside a payload view.

Commit ordering is an observation. The payload view is read inside the save sequence, and so is the change document write. In my tests the change document was always there. I have found no documentation confirming that ordering, and a violation would mean a silently missing event.

And the honest one. C_SalesChangeDocItemDEX is annotated #EXTRACTION_DATA_SOURCE and I used it as an event payload source. It activates and it works, but that is not obviously what it is for. If anyone from SAP can say whether this is supported, or whether a released change document interface view for SD is planned, I would like to know.

Why bother

If you build event driven integration on S/4HANA and only care about specific fields, this moves the decision to where it belongs. The events that do not matter never leave the system.

It works for any field that writes change documents, which is most of them.

entry.title: An AI agent that rebooks passengers in ABAP, and waits for your approval first
entry.content:
A flight is cancelled and nine passengers have to be moved. There are only six free seats on the alternative flights, spread over three flights and three days. Someone has to decide who goes where, and someone has to make the change in the booking system.

That is a good task for an agent, as long as the agent isn't the one who presses the button. With the September 2026 release of CAP, the agent and the approval step can both be declared in CDS. I built a small demo, Flight Rescue, to see how far that gets you against a real ABAP system:

  • A CAP-level agent (@cap-js/agents) reads the affected bookings from an ABAP Platform Trial through a custom RAP service.
  • It proposes a rebooking plan and pauses for a dispatcher to approve (@ Agent.hitl).
  • Only after approval does CAP call a RAP action that moves each booking, one at a time.
  • A SAPUI5 cockpit shows the whole flow on one screen, including a seat map that fills up as ABAP confirms each move.

The cockpit with the agent's plan waiting for approval. Each dot on the right is a seat, read from ABAP; the orange ones are the nine affected passengers.

 

What's new in the September 2026 release, and what this demo uses


FeatureStatus in the releaseUsed here for
CAP-level agents (@cap-js/agents ) : @ Agent on a CDS service gives you a ReAct loop in your CAP server, served over A2AGamma (Node.js); Java is AlphaThe rebooking agent
@ Agent.hitl: human approval before an action runsNode.js onlyApprove or reject the plan
MCP adapter: the generic describe, query (now in CQL) and call toolsGenerally availableThe agent's tools, generated from the service
Chat preview for local developmentAlpha / experimentalTesting the agent before the cockpit existed

 

Everything else is plain CAP and RAP: a remote OData V4 service, an in-memory SQLite database for the plans, and a freestyle SAPUI5 page.

 

The architecture

The ABAP side is a custom RAP business object over a Z copy of /DMO/BOOKING. It has one action, rebook, which moves a booking to another flight. The action checks everything itself: the booking still exists and isn't cancelled, it is still on the expected flight, and the target flight exists, flies the same route and has a free seat. CAP never writes to ABAP in any other way.

 

1. An agent is a CDS service with one annotation

This is the whole agent definition, apart from the system prompt:

/**
 * You are the rebooking assistant for cancelled flights. ...
 * (the doc comment is the system prompt)
 */
@agent
@agent.connect: 'none'
@requires: 'Dispatcher'
service RebookAgentService {
  @readonly entity Disruptions as projection on fr.Disruptions excluding { plans };
  @readonly entity Plans       as projection on fr.Plans excluding { agentTask };
  @readonly entity PlanItems   as projection on fr.PlanItems;

  /** The disruption, its affected bookings and the only valid alternative flights. Changes nothing. */
  function disruptionImpact(disruption : UUID) returns fr.Impact;

  /** Save a Pending rebooking plan. Nothing changes in the booking system. */
  action proposeRebooking(disruption : UUID, assignments : many fr.Assignment, rationale : String) returns fr.ProposalResult;

  /** Request human approval to run this task's Pending plan in the booking system. */
  @AGent.hitl
  action applyRebooking(plan : UUID) returns fr.ApplyResult;
}

When the server starts, the plugin does three things:

  1. It builds tools from the service: the generic MCP tools describe and query for the entities, and one tool per function or action.
  2. It runs a ReAct loop with the configured LLM.
  3. It serves the agent over A2A at /a2a/rebook-agent, plus the chat preview in development.

The LLM comes from cds.requires.llm. In this demo it points at the Anthropic model implementation that ships with the plugin, with claude-opus-5-5, because I ran everything locally. On SAP BTP you'd use the documented kind: aicore instead, which goes through SAP AI Core and is the default in the production and hybrid profiles. In development, the default kind: auto picks up the credentials of a local Claude Code or OpenCode installation, so you may not need any configuration at all.

@requires: 'Dispatcher' works as it does on any CAP service: a user without the role can't talk to the agent at all.

What I like most here is that the agent can read only the three projections and call the three operations. It has no SQL connection, no generic HTTP client and no ABAP credentials. If something isn't in the service, the agent can't do it.

Two notes on the annotations:

  • @ Agent.connect: 'none' keeps the agent narrow: no extra MCP servers, no subagents. The plugin reads this annotation, but at the time of writing it isn't in the capire guide, so check that it still exists before you rely on it.
  • I included no AGENTS.md, on purpose. The release also lets you put an AGENTS.md and skills/*/SKILL.md files next to the service. When AGENTS.md is present, the plugin builds the agent from that directory instead of the generic ReAct agent. That is the right choice for a rich assistant like the XTravels sample. For a single, narrow job, the service's doc comment as the system prompt was enough.

 

2. The model sees CQL, not OData

The MCP adapter is generally available (GA) in this release, and its query tool now takes CQL. In the server log you can watch the agent work it out: it describes the entity, queries it, and then calls the custom functions:

[agents] - RebookAgentService request { method: 'message/send', text: 'LH 0402 on 2026-12-31 is cancelled. Rebook the passengers.' }
[mcp] - RebookAgentService describe { entities: [ 'Disruptions' ] }
[mcp] - RebookAgentService query {
  cql: "SELECT ID, carrierId, connectionId, flightDate, airportFrom, airportTo, reason, status FROM Disruptions
        WHERE carrierId = 'LH' AND connectionId = '0402' AND flightDate = '2026-12-31'"
}
[mcp] - RebookAgentService - call disruptionImpact { disruption: '4538ad9d-…' }
[mcp] - RebookAgentService - call proposeRebooking { disruption: '4538ad9d-…', assignments: [ … ] }

This log is unedited apart from line breaks. I didn't write any tool code for describe or query.

 

What the ReAct loop is doing here

ReAct stands for "Reasoning and Acting": the model works in rounds. In each round it reads the conversation so far and either asks for a tool call or writes its final answer. The server runs the tool, adds the result to the conversation, and the next round starts. The model never executes anything itself. It only asks, and CAP decides.

The loop runs inside the CAP server. The plugin builds it with LangGraph and keeps the conversation and checkpoints in CAP's database. In every round the model gets the same three things:

  • the system prompt, which is the service's doc comment
  • the five tools generated from the service
  • the conversation so far, including every earlier tool result

The log above, round by round:

     
RoundThe model asks forWhat CAP does
1describe DisruptionsReturns the entity's fields
2query with a CQL SELECT … FROM Disruptions WHERE …Runs it on the service, with the dispatcher's authorisations
3disruptionImpactMy handler reads the bookings from ABAP and returns the 9 bookings and the only valid alternatives
4proposeRebookingMy handler checks the plan against the rules and saves it as Pending
5applyRebookingDoesn't run it. The loop stops here and waits for a human (next section)
6after ApproveRuns the action, which moves the bookings in ABAP
7the final answerShows the summary in the chat

 

The model decides the order of the calls, so two runs can take different paths and produce different plans. What it may call is fixed, though. There are only five tools, and each one goes through ordinary CAP handlers and @requires checks.

 

3. @ Agent.hitl: the pause

Here is the part that makes this usable for something that changes business data. Because applyRebooking is annotated @ Agent.hitl, the action doesn't run when the model decides to call it. Instead, the A2A task goes to the input-required state, and the pending call (including the plan ID) is in the task's status message:

task.status.state                                   // 'input-required'
task.status.message.metadata['sap.cds.agents.hitl']
    .actionRequests[0].args.plan                    // the plan waiting for approval

Any A2A client can then resume the same task with an approval or a rejection. In the cockpit, those are two JSON-RPC message/send calls:

approve: task => send([{ kind: 'text', text: 'approve' }], task),
reject: (task, message) => send([{ kind: 'data', data: { decisions: [{ type: 'reject', message }] } }], task)

send adds the task's taskId and contextId.

Prompts aren't a good control, but this is. The system prompt does tell the model not to ask for confirmation in text, but the guarantee doesn't depend on the model following it. Whatever the model writes, the action body doesn't run until a human resumes the task. With audit logging set up (I didn't in this demo), the plugin also records each approval or rejection as an AgentTaskResumed event.

I only had to put a UI on top. The cockpit shows the paused plan as a card with Approve and Reject, grouped by target flight, with the number of unassigned passengers and the agent's reasoning.

The paused task as the dispatcher sees it. The reasoning is the model's own; the numbers come from the server.

 

4. Approval

The domain rules are ordinary CAP code, and the agent can only choose among options the server has already checked:

  • disruptionImpact returns the affected bookings and the only valid alternatives: same route, same day up to two days later, seats left after other pending plans.
  • proposeRebooking refuses any booking, flight or seat count outside that list. It saves a Pending plan and changes nothing in ABAP.
  • The plan is bound to its agent task. The A2A task ID travels server-side, so it is never a tool argument. A resumed call that points at a different plan is refused (NOT_REVIEWED).
  • Each booking is moved with its expected current flight. If someone changed the booking in ABAP after the proposal, that one fails alone (STALE), and the rest still apply.
  • The model sees no customer data, only travel and booking IDs, flights and seat counts.

Because the agent is a CAP service, I could also tighten the generated tools with a normal CAP handler. The plugin raises a buildTools event, so a few lines check the tool list against an allowlist at startup and make the tool schemas strict, so unknown arguments are refused rather than dropped:

this.on('buildTools', async (req, next) => {
  const tools = await next()
  if (tools.map(t => t.name).join() !== TOOLS.join()) throw new Error('Agent tools differ from the allowlist')
  for (const t of tools) if (OPERATIONS.includes(t.name)) t.schema = t.schema.strict()
  return tools
})

 

5. Run against a real ABAP system

The agent's data access goes through one CAP remote service, ZFR_REBOOK. Its CDS model matches the $metadata of the published OData V4 binding.

  • Without credentials: cds watch mocks the service from the same contract. The mock applies the same checks and messages as the ABAP action, so the whole flow runs offline. The tests use a scripted model, so they need no API key either.
  • With credentials: set ABAP_URL, SAP_USER and SAP_PASSWORD as environment variables, and the same code talks to the ABAP Platform Trial.

In the run I recorded, the scenario was LH 0402 on FRA–EWR, with 9 bookings in three travels and 6 free seats on five alternatives. The agent proposed the following, and left 3 bookings unassigned with a reason:

  • travel 90000003 (2 bookings) → UA 0043, same day
  • travel 90000002 (3 bookings) → LH 0402, the next day
  • one booking of travel 90000001 → UA 0043, the next day

The plan isn't scripted. In the take shown in the GIF at the top, the agent split travel 90000001 across two flights and left travel 90000002 unassigned instead. Both plans stay within the seats the server listed, and that's the point: the model chooses, the server decides what it may choose from.

After Approve, the table in ABAP showed exactly those six moves, and the three alternatives were full. A Reject on a fresh scenario left all nine bookings where they were.

Before: the disruption is declared and nobody has moved yet.

After Approve: six orange seats have moved to the alternatives, which are now full, and three passengers are still on the cancelled flight. The agent's summary is in the chat.

 

Lessons learned

  • The A2A endpoint and browser logins. With mocked or basic authentication, the A2A endpoint answers 401 without a WWW-Authenticate challenge, so a browser never sends it the login it already uses for the OData service. A three-line middleware that adds the Basic challenge fixed it for local development. A deployed app with tokens doesn't need it.
  • RAP and leading zeros. The OData V4 binding returns NUMC fields without leading zeros ("TravelId":"4506") but accepts them with. I pad them in the one module that talks to ABAP.
  • Messages from RAP are cut at 50 characters when created with new_message_with_text, so keep the action's texts short. They end up in front of the dispatcher, and in front of the model.

 

A word on the SAP API Policy

The CAP documentation is explicit: CAP-level agents are meant for exposing custom CAP application services. They are not an SAP-endorsed pathway for agentic access to SAP Application APIs (section 2.2.2 of the SAP API Policy). This demo stays inside that line. The agent exposes only this app's own services, and the ABAP side is a custom Z RAP service over custom tables. For agentic access to SAP Application APIs, the CAP docs point to the reference architectures in the SAP Architecture Center.

 

Try it yourself

  • Code: https://github.com/Kamilkov/flight-rescue.git 
  • CAP release notes, September 2026: https://cap.cloud.sap/docs/releases/2026/sep26
  • CAP-level agents guide: https://cap.cloud.sap/docs/guides/ai/cap-agents
  • MCP adapter guide: https://cap.cloud.sap/docs/guides/ai/cap-mcp

entry.title: Parallel Processing Technique and Its Application in a Business Process
entry.content:
Summary
