  • They are triggered by side effects: when the user changes a source field (e.g. trip description), the recommendation function runs and proposes values for the target field (e.g. trip category).
  • They integrate seamlessly with the RAP programming model. No custom UI development required. Zero. Nada.

Figure 1: Fiori Input Assistance implemented with RAP recommendations

How It Works: The Architecture

The implementation involves three layers:

  1. Behavior Definition – Declare which fields receive recommendations and define the recommendation function.
  2. Behavior Implementation – Implement the recommendation logic in the behavior pool, using the ABAP AI SDK to call an LLM for intelligent categorization.
  3. Projection Behavior Definition – Expose the recommendations in the projection layer for the Fiori UI.

If you've built a RAP Business Object before, this will feel very familiar. It's the same layered pattern, just with AI sprinkled on top.

Step 1: Define Recommendations in the Behavior Definition

In your behavior definition, you mark the target field as relevant for recommendations, declare a recommendation function and define a side effect on which the recommendation function should be triggered. This tells the RAP framework: whenever the user changes the “title” field, execute function GetRecommendedValuesFunction and propose values for attribute “type”. The user types "Customer workshop in Berlin" and the system immediately suggests "Customer-facing". It almost feels like the system is reading the user's mind, except it's reading their input field.

define behavior for ZR_AITRIP alias Trip
{
  //Define for which fields an recommendation output is generated
  field ( recommendations ) Type;

  //Define the recommendation function itself
  recommendation function GetRecommendedValuesFunction;

  //Define the trigger (e.g. other context field)
  side effects
  {
    recommendation function GetRecommendedValuesFunction 
      executed on field Title;
  }
}

Step 2: Implement the Recommendation Logic

In the behavior pool, you implement the recommendation function. This is where the ABAP AI SDK comes in. You use the completion API to ask an LLM to categorize the trip based on the available context:

  1. Read the current entity data (description, destination, etc.)
  2. Build a prompt with the trip context, based on your system's master data
  3. Call the ABAP AI SDK Completion API
  4. Parse the LLM response
  5. Return the recommended value(s) with scores

The recommendation function returns a list of proposed values, each with a score and a flag indicating whether it's the suggested (top-ranked) value. The Fiori UI renders these as input assistance. The user can accept, modify, or override the suggestion. The AI proposes, the human decides. As it should be.

The full implementation:

class lhc_zr_aitrip definition inheriting from cl_abap_behavior_handler.

  private section.

    methods get_global_authorizations for global authorization
      importing
        request requested_authorizations for Trip
        result  result.

    methods GetRecommendedValuesFunction for read
      keys for function Trip~GetRecommendedValuesFunction result result.

    methods build_recommendation_prompt
      importing title         type string
      returning value(result) type string.

    methods get_type_recommendation
      importing prompt        type string
      returning value(result) type string.

endclass.


class lhc_zr_aitrip implementation.

  method get_global_authorizations.
    " demo only: open for all users - add real authorization checks before productive use
    result-%create = if_abap_behv=>auth-allowed.
  endmethod.

  method GetRecommendedValuesFunction.

    result = corresponding #( keys ).

    read entities of zr_aitrip in local mode
      entity Trip
        fields ( Title ) with corresponding #( keys )
      result data(trips)
      failed failed.

    loop at result assigning field-symbol(<result>).

      read table trips with table key id components %tky = <result>-%tky into data(trip).
      check sy-subrc = 0 and trip-Title is not initial.

      data(type_prompt)      = build_recommendation_prompt( conv #( trip-Title ) ).
      data(recommended_type) = get_type_recommendation( type_prompt ).

      check recommended_type is not initial.

      <result>-%param = value #(
        trip-type = value #( (
          score     = '1.0'
          value     = recommended_type
          suggested = 'X' ) ) ).

    endloop.

  endmethod.


  method build_recommendation_prompt.

    result = |Derive a trip category based on the given trip title: | &&
             |{ title }| && cl_abap_char_utilities=>cr_lf &&
             |The following trip categories exist: C (Customer facing), I (Internal).| && cl_abap_char_utilities=>cr_lf &&
             |Please only answer with 'C' or 'I' as a single character.|.

  endmethod.


  method get_type_recommendation.

    try.
        data(api)                = cl_aic_islm_compl_api_factory=>get( )->create_instance( 'ZINTS_TRAVELAPP' ).
        data(message_container)  = api->create_message_container( ).
        message_container->add_user_message( prompt ).

        result = api->execute_for_messages( message_container )->get_completion( ).

      catch cx_aic_api_factory cx_aic_prompt_template cx_aic_completion_api.
        " recommendations are optional - on failure the field simply gets no suggested value
    endtry.

  endmethod.

endclass.

Step 3: Expose in the Projection

Make sure to expose the functionality in your UI projection by using “use recommendations;”. And that's it. The Fiori UI picks up the recommendation pattern automatically. No custom UI code, no frontend development, no begging a UI5 developer for help.

The Beauty of It

The beauty of RAP recommendations is the zero-effort UX integration. You implement the intelligence once in the behavior pool, and every Fiori Elements UI that consumes your RAP Business Object automatically benefits from the recommendations. It's the RAP philosophy at its finest: define the behavior, and the framework handles the presentation. And because the recommendation logic uses the ABAP AI SDK, you can switch from a deterministic rule-based approach to a generative AI approach (or vice versa) without changing the behavior definition or the UI. The abstraction is clean, the separation of concerns is real, and your future self will thank your present self for the architecture.

 

Use Case 2: Receipt Data Extraction

The Problem

After a business trip, the employee needs to submit expense reports with receipts attached. Hotel invoices, restaurant bills, taxi receipts. Today, the employee manually types in every field: vendor name, amount, currency, date, tax, category. It's tedious, error-prone, and, let's be honest, the reason most people procrastinate on their expense reports for weeks. Some of us have receipts from trips that happened so long ago that the ink has faded. Not speaking from personal experience, of course.

What if the employee could simply upload a receipt image and the system would extract the relevant data automatically?

Figure 2: AI-generated invoice

The Solution: Document Extraction with the ABAP AI SDK

This use case leverages the ABAP AI SDK's ability to send content, including file-based content, to an LLM and receive structured data back. The flow is:

  1. The user uploads a receipt (image) through the Fiori application.
  2. The ABAP application receives the file content.
  3. The ABAP AI SDK sends the file content along with a structured prompt to the LLM (via the Generative AI Hub).
  4. The LLM extracts key fields: vendor name, amount, currency, date, tax amount, expense category.
  5. The extracted data is returned to the ABAP application and pre-fills the expense line item.

The user uploads a crumpled taxi receipt, and five seconds later all the fields are filled in correctly. That's the kind of user experience that makes people actually submit their expense reports on time.

Figure 3: Extracted data from file

Step 1: Enhance the CDS Data Model for File Upload

Before we can extract anything, we need to give users a way to upload their receipts. In RAP, file uploads are modelled as Large Objects (LOBs) using the @Semantics.largeObject annotation in your CDS view. This tells the framework to treat the field as a binary stream and render it as a file upload control in the Fiori UI (SAP Help, Working with Large Objects). First, your database table needs three fields: the binary content itself, a MIME type field, and a file name field. Then, in your CDS entity, you annotate them accordingly:

@Semantics.largeObject: {
    acceptableMimeTypes: [ 'image/*', 'application/*' ],
    cacheControl.maxAge: #MEDIUM,
    contentDispositionPreference: #INLINE,
    fileName: 'UploadedReceiptFileName',
    mimeType: 'UploadedReceiptMimeType'
}
UploadedReceipt,

@Semantics.mimeType: true
UploadedReceiptMimeType,

UploadedReceiptFileName,

Let's break down what's happening here:

  • UploadedReceipt is the actual LOB field that stores the binary content of the uploaded file. The @Semantics.largeObject annotation binds it to its MIME type and file name fields, and defines which file types are accepted.
  • acceptableMimeTypes controls what the user can upload. In our case, image/* covers photos of receipts (JPEG, PNG, etc.) and application/* covers PDFs and other document formats. If you want to be more restrictive, you can specify individual MIME types like 'image/jpeg', 'application/pdf'.
  • UploadedReceiptMimeType stores the MIME type of the uploaded file and must carry the @Semantics.mimeType: true annotation. This is what the framework uses to know how to handle the file.
  • UploadedReceiptFileName stores the original file name. Technically optional, but very much recommended, because your users will appreciate seeing "taxi_receipt_berlin.pdf" instead of a cryptic binary blob identifier.
  • contentDispositionPreference: #INLINE tells the browser to display the file directly when possible (e.g. images and PDFs), rather than forcing a download.

Once these annotations are in place, the Fiori Elements automatically renders an upload control on the Object Page. No UI5 coding, no custom frontend logic. The user clicks upload, picks a file, and the binary content flows into your RAP Business Object. If you've ever implemented file upload the "classic" way in SAP, you'll appreciate how clean this is.

Step 2: Extract Data with the ABAP AI SDK

With the receipt uploaded and stored in the LOB field, the extraction can begin. The implementation combines the file content from the RAP entity with the ABAP AI SDK Completion API. You read the binary content from the LOB, and send it along with a structured extraction prompt through the SDK.

An execution flow could look like this:

  1. Read the uploaded receipt content from the entity (UploadedReceipt field)
  2. Convert to base64 encoding
  3. Build a structured extraction prompt:    
    'Extract the following fields from this receipt: vendor_name, amount, currency, date, tax_amount, category. Return the result as JSON'.
  4. Call the ABAP AI SDK Completion API with the prompt and the file content
  5. Parse the JSON response
  6. Map extracted fields to the expense line item entity

The full implementation:

class lhc_expense definition inheriting from cl_abap_behavior_handler.

  private section.

    types: begin of ty_reference_lists,
             transaction_types type string,
             categories        type string,
           end of ty_reference_lists.

    methods extractData for determine on modify
      keys for Expense~extractData.

    methods get_reference_data_lists
      returning value(result) type ty_reference_lists.

    methods build_extraction_prompt
      importing reference_lists type ty_reference_lists
      returning value(result)   type string.

    methods call_ai_extraction
      importing receipt       type xstring
                prompt        type string
      returning value(result) type string
      raising   cx_aic_completion_api
                cx_aic_api_factory.

    methods parse_extraction_response
      importing json    type string
      changing  expense type any
      raising   cx_root.

endclass.


class lhc_expense implementation.

  method extractData.

    read entities of zr_aitrip in local mode
         entity Expense all fields with corresponding #( keys )
         result data(expenses).

    check expenses is not initial.

    data(reference_lists) = get_reference_data_lists( ).
    data(prompt)          = build_extraction_prompt( reference_lists ).

    data updates type table for update zr_aitrip\\Expense.

    loop at expenses assigning field-symbol(<expense>).

      if <expense>-UploadedReceipt is initial.
        append value #( %tky = <expense>-%tky
                         %msg = new_message_with_text( severity = if_abap_behv_message=>severity-error
                                                        text     = 'No receipt uploaded - nothing to extract' ) )
          to reported-expense.
        continue.
      endif.

      try.
          data(answer) = call_ai_extraction( receipt = <expense>-UploadedReceipt
                                              prompt  = prompt ).

          parse_extraction_response( exporting json    = answer
                                      changing  expense = <expense> ).

          append corresponding #( <expense> ) to updates.

        catch cx_aic_completion_api cx_aic_api_factory into data(ai_error).
          append value #( %tky = <expense>-%tky
                           %msg = new_message_with_text( severity = if_abap_behv_message=>severity-error
                                                          text     = |Receipt could not be processed by the AI service: { ai_error->get_text( ) }| ) )
            to reported-expense.

        catch cx_root into data(parse_error).
          append value #( %tky = <expense>-%tky
                           %msg = new_message_with_text( severity = if_abap_behv_message=>severity-error
                                                          text     = |Receipt data could not be interpreted: { parse_error->get_text( ) }| ) )
            to reported-expense.
      endtry.

    endloop.

    check updates is not initial.

    modify entities of zr_aitrip in local mode
       entity Expense
       update fields ( ExpenseDescription TransactionType Category Amount Currency )
       with updates.

  endmethod.


  method get_reference_data_lists.

    select transactiontype, description from zr_transactiontype into table @DATA(transaction_types).
    loop at transaction_types reference into data(transaction_type).
      result-transaction_types = result-transaction_types &&
        |{ transaction_type->transactiontype } ({ transaction_type->description }),|.
    endloop.

    select category, description from zr_category into table @DATA(categories).
    loop at categories reference into data(category).
      result-categories = result-categories && |{ category->category } ({ category->description }),|.
    endloop.

  endmethod.


  method build_extraction_prompt.

    result = |Analyze the attached receipt and extract the following information.| && cl_abap_char_utilities=>cr_lf
          && |Do NOT wrap the response in markdown. Respond in valid JSON.| && cl_abap_char_utilities=>cr_lf
          && |\{ | && cl_abap_char_utilities=>cr_lf
          && |"TransactionType" :"",| && cl_abap_char_utilities=>cr_lf
          && |"Category" :"",| && cl_abap_char_utilities=>cr_lf
          && |"ExpenseDescription" :"",| && cl_abap_char_utilities=>cr_lf
          && |"Amount" :"",| && cl_abap_char_utilities=>cr_lf
          && |"Currency" :""| && cl_abap_char_utilities=>cr_lf
          && |\}| && cl_abap_char_utilities=>cr_lf
          && |The following TransactionTypes exist in the system: { reference_lists-transaction_types }| && cl_abap_char_utilities=>cr_lf
          && |The following Categories exist in the system: { reference_lists-categories }|.

  endmethod.


  method call_ai_extraction.

    data(api)               = cl_aic_islm_compl_api_factory=>get( )->create_instance( 'ZINTS_TRAVELAPP' ).
    data(message_container) = api->create_message_container( ).

    message_container->add_user_media_message(
      )->add_media( aic_media_type=>image_webp
      )->set_media_data( cl_web_http_utility=>encode_x_base64( receipt )
      )->add_text( prompt ).

    result = api->execute_for_messages( message_container )->get_completion( ).

  endmethod.


  method parse_extraction_response.

    /ui2/cl_json=>deserialize( exporting json        = json
                                         pretty_name = /ui2/cl_json=>pretty_mode-none
                               changing  data        = expense ).

  endmethod.

endclass.

The extraction can be triggered as a RAP determination (automatically when the file is uploaded), as a RAP action (explicitly by the user pressing an "Extract" button), or even through an event-driven side effect that fires after the upload completes. All three options are valid RAP patterns, and the right choice depends on your UX preferences. Personally, I like the determination approach: the user uploads the file, and by the time they look at the form fields, they're already filled in. A small moment of delight in an otherwise tedious process.

Orchestration Adds Enterprise Readiness

This is where the orchestration capabilities mentioned earlier become critical. Receipts may contain sensitive personal data: credit card numbers, home addresses, personal phone numbers. By enabling Data Masking in the orchestration configuration, you ensure that such data is redacted before it reaches the LLM. No code changes required, it's a configuration in the intelligent scenario. Similarly, Document Grounding can be used to provide additional context to the LLM (for example, your company's expense categories and vendor master data), improving extraction accuracy significantly. The LLM doesn't just guess "Restaurant" as a category, it picks the exact category code from your company's chart of accounts.

The Beauty of It

Receipt extraction is a high-volume, low-complexity task that AI handles extremely well. Every minute saved on manual data entry is a minute your employees spend on work that actually matters. And because the extraction runs inside ABAP, not in an external service that your users need to learn, the integration is invisible. The user uploads a file, the fields fill themselves. That's it. That's the entire (very simple) user story.

 

Additional References

You want directly jump start into an own implementation? Go for it! In case any questions arise within this journey, feel free to check out the following additional references:

  • ABAP AI SDK, SAP Help
  • Set Up ABAP AI SDK powered by ISLM, SAP Help
  • Defining RAP Recommendations in the Behavior Definition, SAP Help
  • RAP Recommendations, SAP Community Blog
  • Implement a Simple Custom ABAP AI Scenario, SAP Developers Tutorial

 

Cheerio ABAP Folks!

entry.title: From SOAP to RAP: Choosing a Web Service Technology in S/4HANA
entry.content:
1. Introduction

Over the years, SAP has introduced several generations of web service technology, and anyone starting a new integration project on S/4HANA today can easily lose track of which option actually fits the use case. Should an existing BAPI be released as a SOAP service? Should a classic OData v2 service be built with the Gateway Service Builder? Or is it better to go straight to RAP and OData v4, and if so, which flavor of RAP? This article is a practical, comparison-oriented overview for architects and developers who need to make that call. It is not a deep dive into any of the single technologies.

Scope. To keep the comparison practical, this article is limited to HTTP-based technologies that run entirely inside the S/4HANA system. In other words, it covers options that work without provisioning separate components such as SAP BTP Integration Suite or Event Mesh.

Read vs. write. All example calls are deliberately read-only. This keeps the examples short and comparable across technologies, without the extra complexity of create/update/delete semantics. Every technology section nevertheless explains how write access differs, so the full picture is covered.

Running example. To make the comparison concrete, every section uses the same fictional scenario: retrieving a business partner’s name and address. The data comes from the tables BUT000 (general business partner data), ADRC (address data) and BUT020 (mapping between the two). This is a small join, but a realistic and common one in S/4HANA projects, and complex enough to show how each technology copes with more than a flat, single-table lookup.

A decision matrix at the end of the article compares the technologies across several criteria: future viability, how much of the interface is defined by the developer versus dictated by the respective framework, the degree of manual implementation effort and the technical basis involved.

 

2. SOAP (RFC/BAPI released as a web service)

How it works: This is the most traditional way of exposing web service in S/4 HANA. An existing RFC-enabled function module or BAPI is released via the SOA-Manager, which generates a WSDL from the function module’s signature (import/export parameters, tables etc.). The function module itself is the implementation, so no additional code has to be written.

Implementation: First, an RFC-enabled function module is selected for exposure, either a standard one or a self-written one. A wizard in the Function Builder then creates the service definition. Alternatively, the service definition can be created in the Object Navigator (SE80). In both cases, the service is subsequently configured and activated as a runtime service in the SOA-Manager.

For the running example, this could mean either developing a custom function module that performs the table join, or choosing a standard one such as the BAPI BAPI_BUPA_ADDRESS_GETDETAIL.

Example call: Unlike the REST-style URLs discussed below, the endpoint of a SOAP service can contain multiple operations. The operation to be called is specified inside the XML body. A fictional endpoint might look like this:

POST https://<system>.example.com:44300/sap/bc/srt/rfc/sap/z_bp_address_read/300/z_bp_address_read/z_bp_address_read

Content-Type: text/xml; charset=utf-8

The HTTP request body wraps the operation and its import parameters in a <soap:Envelope>/<soap:Body> structure. The response mirrors the export parameters and tables back as XML.

Write access: For create/update, a write-enabled function module is released in the same way as a read-only one, for example the BAPIs BAPI_BUPA_CREATE and BAPI_BUPA_ADDRESS_ADD. Transaction handling is usually done server-side inside the function module, although client-steered commit handling is possible as well.

Error handling: Errors can surface on three different levels: Technical failures are reported via the HTTP status code (e.g. 500). SOAP Faults are standardized error structures inside the SOAP envelope, containing a fault code and message, and are usually returned together with HTTP status 500, for example for invalid request XML or an uncaught exception in the function module. Business errors such as “business partner not found” often arrive as a valid response with a RETURN table (e.g. BAPIRET2) and a message type like E, but can also be raised as SOAP Faults. Consumers therefore need to evaluate the HTTP status, the SOAP Fault and the business-level return structure.

Other features: The service’s capabilities are described in a metadata file following the Web Service Description Language (WSDL). Further features, such as switching between XML and JSON, filtering, or paging for high-volume calls, are either not feasible or have to be implemented manually in each function module.

When to use it: SOAP-released BAPIs can mainly be understood as legacy. SAP does not recommend this approach for new development, and hasn’t for some time. It can still be a reasonable choice when a function module already does exactly what is required and no suitable CDS views or standard OData services exist. In most other cases, the strategically recommended path is found in the later sections of this article, particularly RAP with OData v4.

 

3. OData v2 (SAP Gateway / SEGW)

How it works: The SAP Gateway Service Builder introduced a structured way of exposing data as a REST-based service following the OData v2 protocol. Entities and their relationships are modelled in transaction SEGW, while the actual data retrieval is implemented manually in generated ABAP classes, typically by redefining methods such as GET_ENTITYSET or GET_ENTITY. The resulting service follows OData v2 conventions for addressing, filtering and other query options.

Implementation: The typical path starts with creating a project in the Service Builder (SEGW), where the entity types and entity sets are defined. In the running example these would be BusinessPartner and BusinessPartnerAddress, including their relationship. After generating the development artifacts, the data provider class is implemented, for example by calling a suitable read BAPI or by selecting directly from the underlying tables or views inside GET_ENTITYSET. Finally, the service is activated and registered in /IWFND/MAINT_SERVICE, which makes it callable.

Example call: OData’s URL conventions make reading a specific business partner and its address look like this:

GET https://<system>.example.com/sap/opu/odata/sap/ZBP_ADDRESS_V2/BusinessPartnerAddressSet('P1001')?$expand=_toAddress

Accept: application/json

Since this is a GET call, no HTTP body is required for read access.

Error handling: Errors come back as standard HTTP status codes (404 for a business partner that doesn’t exist, 400 for a malformed filter, and so on), together with an OData-standard JSON or XML error message in the HTTP body containing an error message and an error code.

Write access: Create, update and delete operations map to the standard HTTP verbs (POST, PUT, DELETE) against the entity set. They are implemented by redefining the corresponding methods (CREATE_ENTITY, UPDATE_ENTITY, DELETE_ENTITY) in the same data provider class. The content of the respective data set is sent in the HTTP body.

Other features: OData v2 comes with built-in query options such as filtering on specific fields, selecting data by key or regular fields, and paging. In SEGW, however, most of these must be implemented manually in the data provider classes. On the output side, both XML and JSON are supported, with JSON being the de facto default in most implementations today. OData v2 also provides a service description in the form of an EDMX file following the Common Schema Definition Language (CSDL), which can be retrieved by appending $metadata to the service root.

When to use it: OData v2 via SEGW is stable, and many systems rely on it, but it is no longer where SAP’s strategic development effort goes. For new services, SAP steers toward RAP. Note that RAP can also expose services via OData v2, so "OData v2" and "SEGW" are not strictly the same decision.

 

4. Custom REST (ICF handler)

How it works: This option builds on a rather basic framework: a handler class is registered directly in the Internet Communication Framework (SICF). The handler class acts as a dispatcher. It interprets incoming calls and selects and executes a suitable resource class. There is no metadata, no generated create/read/update/delete (CRUD) functionality and no standardized query syntax. The developer decides on the URL structure, the payload shape, the HTTP verbs used, and how (or whether) to support filtering and paging, down to the interpretation and setting of each individual HTTP header. This makes it the most flexible option covered here, and also the one with the least built-in support.

Implementation: The starting point is a handler class implementing the interface IF_HTTP_EXTENSION. This class interprets the service-specific part of the URI and matches it against registered patterns, similar to regular expressions. When the URI matches a pattern, the resource class registered for that pattern is called. Patterns can contain variables, for instance /client/{clientid: [1-9][0-9]*}. A call ending in /client/4711 would invoke the registered resource class with the parameter clientid set to 4711.

The resource class must implement the interface IF_REST_RESOURCE, in which the methods for the individual HTTP verbs can be redefined (e.g. IF_REST_RESOURCE~GET). Inside these methods, the variables from the URI are available, as well as other inputs such as HTTP headers, the HTTP body and query parameters. After parsing these, the business logic is executed, and the HTTP status code, response headers and response body are set by the custom code.

Example call: Since there is no protocol convention to follow, the shape is entirely up to the developer. A call might look like this:

GET https://<system>.example.com/sap/bc/zbp_address/Partner/P1001

Accept: application/json

Error handling: Also entirely custom: the development team decides which HTTP status codes to return and how to structure the error body.

Write access: No different in principle from read access. The development team handles the HTTP verbs and payload parsing, and is fully responsible for locking, transactional consistency and validation, since none of the generic RAP or Gateway services apply here.

Other features: Features such as filtering or paging must be implemented from scratch. The response format is entirely free (JSON, XML or anything else). The response body is serialized manually, for JSON for example often with the class /ui2/cl_json.

When to use it: This option is most sensible when a use case genuinely doesn’t fit the standard interfaces, for example because of a highly custom payload shape, a non-CRUD-style API, or a need for tight control over the exact response format. It comes, however, at the price of conceptualizing and implementing a lot of different features that come for free elsewhere.

 

5. RAP (ABAP RESTful Application Programming Model) / OData v4

RAP is SAP’s current strategic model for building services, and the one most closely tied to the Clean Core principle in S/4HANA and to ABAP Cloud. Rather than a single technology, RAP is better understood as a framework with one standard implementation style (managed) and two custom implementation styles (custom entity and unmanaged). These styles differ substantially in how much the framework does and how much has to be implemented by hand. All three are introduced together here because they share the same tooling and core concepts.

5.1 Standard (managed) RAP

How it works: This is the standard way of developing in RAP. Core Data Services (CDS) view entities are defined and connected, and a behavior definition marked as managed is added on top. The framework then generates features such as CRUD from declarative annotations, so no read, create or update methods have to be written by hand.

Implementation: The foundation is a virtual data model made up of CDS views along two dimensions. The first dimension consists of three layers of views defined by SAP: basic views, composite views and consumption views. The second dimension is the relationships between the business entities in those views. In the running example, three basic views are created to access the tables BUT000, BUT020 and ADRC. On the interface layer, two views are created: Z_I_PARTNER and Z_I_PARTNER_ADDRESS. The first reads from the BUT000 basic view, while the second joins the data from BUT020 and ADRC. The two interface views are linked by a composition reflecting the parent-child relationship between partner and address. To expose the model, two consumption views are created which are based on the interface views and restrict the exposed fields to only the one’s necessary in the interface. Next, a behavior definition turns the entity model into a business object (BO) by annotating it with a set of keywords describing its features (see below). Finally, a service definition exposes the relevant entities, and a service binding (UI or Web API, OData v2 or v4) makes the service callable from outside. Note that the whole implementation can be done without writing any ABAP code: only CDS views and configuration artifacts are created. However, adding operations on top of CRUD is possible as determinations and actions using ABAP.

Example call: The shape of read access depends on whether OData v2 or v4 is chosen in the service binding. An OData v4 example could look like this:

GET https://<system>.example.com/sap/opu/odata4/sap/zsb_address_v4/srvd/sap/zsd_address/0001/BusinessPartnerAddress('P1001')

Accept: application/json

Error handling: As with SEGW, errors come back as standard HTTP status codes, accompanied by an OData-standard message in the HTTP body containing an error message and an error code.

Write access: Write capabilities are added declaratively through annotations in the behavior definition. This covers create, update and delete, as well as transaction handling and the ability to save draft versions.

Other features: Standard RAP comes with a wide range of built-in features, which are either active by default or can be added via annotations in the behavior definition. Some of them are: (1) paging, including the use of a skip token, (2) automatic generation of key values for new entries, (3) lock handling for concurrent write processes, (4) authorization handling on different levels, (5) automatic switching between XML and JSON response formats (for OData v2).

When to use it: This is the technology SAP actively recommends for new S/4HANA development, and the one best aligned with Clean Core extensibility. If one is starting from scratch and the interface required is about exposing data consisting of different linked entities based on database tables (as opposed to interfaces with rather algorithmic nature), this is the default choice. It does require a change in thinking about interfaces: Instead of one endpoint for each part or angle of the data in a traditional input-output setup, a data model for a whole domain can be exposed. If that model is well structured, many different data needs can be fulfilled simply through the right OData parameters of one interface endpoint. Parameterizing the requests can be a challenge of it’s own, though, because deciding which entities to read, with which fields, in which order and for which filter criteria, can get very complex.

5.2 RAP with custom entity

How it works: Sometimes data doesn’t come from a straightforward CDS view over a database table. It might come from an RFC call to another system, from a computed result, or from a BAPI wrapping complex logic. A custom entity keeps the consistency of RAP and OData (same tooling, same protocol, same annotation model) while the data retrieval is implemented by hand.

Implementation: The entity’s attributes are defined in a custom-entity CDS definition, marked with the annotation @ObjectModel.query.implementedBy, which names a custom ABAP class. Note that, unlike regular CDS views, a custom entity does not rely on a database table or another view. The ABAP class implements the interface IF_RAP_QUERY_PROVIDER. The signature of its method provides all OData parameters sent by the caller, so it is the developer's duty to handle these parameters and to retrieve and return the result data. The custom entity is then exposed through a behavior definition (in this case optional), a service definition and a service binding, just as with standard entities.

Comparison with standard RAP: With a custom entity, the RAP framework still receives and parses the call’s parameters, but reacting to them is up to the developer’s own ABAP logic. Most OData features therefore remain available in principle, but most of them must be programmed manually. This is also why mixing custom and standard entities within a complex virtual data model can be very challenging and is in some cases impossible. A second limitation is that managed custom entities are read-only. For custom RAP developments with write access, unmanaged business objects are the right choice.

When to use it: A useful complement to standard RAP for read-only scenarios in which standard RAP cannot be used. Where possible, however, prefer exposing the full data model over single, isolated custom entities.

5.3 Unmanaged RAP

How it works: This style provides full control over a business object, including all write operations. The data model can be defined with regular CDS views or custom entities. In contrast to managed RAP, however, the transactional behavior (create, update, delete, locking, authorization and saving) is not generated by the framework but implemented manually.

Implementation: The data model is built from regular CDS views or custom entities just as in managed RAP. In the behavior definition, the business object is then marked as unmanaged together with the name of an implementation class. This class contains local classes: one inheriting from CL_ABAP_BEHAVIOR_HANDLER, in which the methods for creating, updating, deleting, locking and authorizations are implemented, and a second one inheriting from CL_ABAP_BEHAVIOR_SAVER, which gives full control over the LUW transaction handling and the actual saving of the data.

Comparison with standard RAP: Compared to standard RAP or custom entities, unmanaged business objects offer the maximum control over functionality, at the cost of considerably more implementation effort. In this respect they are roughly comparable to the custom REST approach described above. The difference is that a custom REST handler is a very loose framework in which almost everything is a free decision, whereas unmanaged business objects come with a much stricter framework. That framework can act as a guardrail for the implementation, but it can also mean implementing functionality the project does not actually need.

Where this stands today: Valid and supported, but with meaningfully more implementation effort than managed RAP. It should be a deliberate choice for cases that need the control, not a default.

 

6 Decision matrix

The matrix below summarizes technical aspects of the technologies as well as the author’s rating on several dimensions. It lists custom entities and unmanaged business objects as separate rows, since their characteristics genuinely diverge from standard RAP.

 

TechnologyImplementation baseMetadata fileStandard/ProtocolRead / Write  possibleError handlingModernizationFlexibilityFramework SupportManual implementation efforts
SOAP with SOAMANAGERABAPWSDLSOAPRead / WriteSemi-standardizedLowHighLowHigh
Odata with SEGWABAPCSDL/EDMXOdata v2Read / WriteStandardizedLowLowMediumHigh
Custom RESTABAPNoneNoneRead / WriteCustomLowHighLowHigh
Standard RAPCDS ViewsCSDL/EDMXOdata v2 / v4Read / WriteStandardizedHighLowHighLow
RAP with custom entitiesCDS Views + ABAPCSDL/EDMXOdata v2 / v4Read onlyStandardizedHighMediumMediumHigh
RAP with unmanaged BOCDS Views + ABAPCSDL/EDMXOdata v2 / v4Read / WriteStandardizedHighMediumMediumHigh

Technical aspects. Implementation base names the languages or artifact types mainly used for the implementation. Metadata file is the machine-readable service description offered by the technology. Standard / protocol is the protocol the service follows. Read / write shows whether the technology supports write operations. Error handling indicates how standardized error handling is supported beyond plain HTTP status codes.

Ratings. Modernity refers to the roadmap communicated by SAP. Flexibility describes the freedom an implementation offers within the technology. Framework support describes how much the framework does for the developer. Manual effort describes how much has to be implemented by hand. The ratings are subjective, as they would be for any other author, and are meant as broad tendencies only. Their values depend on the individual use case. If a function module already exists that does exactly what is required, the implementation effort with SOAP is naturally very low. Conversely, the effort with standard RAP can be high if the required functionality does not fit well into a CRUD and OData scheme. The same applies to flexibility. Unmanaged business objects are rated medium because, despite their manual implementation, the RAP framework still prescribes much more structure than, for example, a custom REST handler.

 

7. Conclusion

The comparison shows that the further one moves from SOAP or Custom REST toward managed RAP, the more the framework takes over and the less control (and boilerplate code) remains for the developer. This reflects the typical trade-off between flexibility and framework support that is inherent in virtually every programming framework.

In line with SAP’s recommendation, RAP, and in particular standard (managed) RAP, should be the strategic default for new, Clean-Core-aligned services on S/4HANA. It is also the area into which SAP directs its tooling and documentation efforts. The other technologies nevertheless remain relevant in specific situations. SOAP-released BAPIs are the fastest way to expose functionality that already exists as a function module, and given their widespread use in existing landscapes, it is unlikely that they will disappear simply because SAP no longer recommends them. OData v2 via SEGW is a reasonable choice when extending an existing Gateway-based landscape. Finally, a custom REST service based on an ICF handler remains an option for requirements that fit no standardized model at all. It trades standardization, such as metadata, paging and error conventions, for flexibility, and this trade-off should be a deliberate decision.

Within RAP, standard RAP, custom entity and unmanaged business objects are not competing alternatives but tools for different situations. Standard RAP is best suited to exposing an entire data model of several interconnected entities with few or no algorithmic requirements. A custom entity is appropriate when the data cannot easily be derived from CDS views over database tables and only needs to be read. An unmanaged business object keeps the CDS-based model but replaces the generated transactional behavior with custom logic. It therefore fits cases in which write operations do not match the generated CRUD model, for example when they involve many case distinctions or the reuse of existing function modules. In each case, the choice follows the same principle: the more of the implementation is taken over by custom logic, the more control is gained, and the more of the framework’s support is given up.

entry.title: ABAP development tools MCP server: Major update available!
entry.content:
Introduction

The ABAP development tools MCP server shipping with the Eclipse plug-in and the VS Code extension is the official MCP server for ABAP development from SAP.  The new version adds a list of much needed tools which makes the server not rely on external tools such as read/edit from the VS Code chat anymore. This means it can now be properly used with all available CLI tools such as Claude Code, Copilot, Codex, OpenCode, .... This is a significant update which will change the way ABAP developers do agentic development with ABAP. In this blog post we want to provide an overview of the server, explain its architecture, the underlying design philosophies, the available features and how to best get started with using it.

General architecture

In general, the MCP server comes bundled with ADT for Eclipse or ADT for VS Code. It runs on the same Java codebase the normal tools run on. This means it "simply" exposes the existing ABAP tools via an MCP interface.

Advantages of this approach:

  1. A mature software stack - The Java codebase driving the server has been used in production for 15+ years.
  2. Compatibility handling - The MCP server supports all ABAP server releases until SAP NetWeaver 7.31 SP04. It runs on the same compatibility layer as ADT for Eclipse. It features support for detecting incompatibilities and will notify users when they need to upgrade to a newer version.
  3. Edge cases covered - It took us years to find and implement all the different edge cases needed for ADT for Eclipse. Features like SAP Solution Manager support, handling of systems in various states (upgrade, no editing allowed, ...) and especially the handling of all the possible error scenarios took quite some time to figure out and implement.
  4. Full connectivity stack - The server offers all connectivity options that ADT for Eclipse provides: RFC, HTTP.
  5. Client side caching - Over the last decade various caching solutions have been implemented on the ADT client side. These range from file caches for reading development objects to optimizing certain backend functionality by using stateful connections. This is the reason why the MCP tools are fast.

Features

System Connectivity

The MCP server re-uses the existing client connectivity stack:

VersionConnectivity configurationSupported connectivity type
ADT for EclipseSystem connections are maintained via ABAP projectsRFC (SSO, Password), Cloud (Http)
ADT for VS CodeSystem connections are maintained via ABAP destinationsRFC (SSO, Password), Cloud (Http)

Safety policy

The server follows a "safety by default" policy. This means everything is switched off by default. It is up to the user to switch on what is needed and manage the associated risks accordingly. It follows the same "human in the loop" principle which applies to AI in general.

Currently, the following configuration options are available:

  • Server switch - In Eclipse and VS Code the server is switched off by default and needs to be explicitly switched on.
  • System allow list - The user needs to specify which ABAP systems can be used.
  • Read only by default - The included ABAP object edit tool is switched off by default. VS Code users need to be aware that the VS Code chat edit tools need to be managed separately as they come from Microsoft.
  • No package allow-listed by default - All editing operations (Create, Edit, Delete [will be added at some point]) need to be allowed for specific packages by default.

The following diagram shows how users can gradually open up the available access.

Tools

Core philosophy:

  • As token efficient as possible - Every tool gets optimized for maximum efficiency while maintaining a solid out of the box experience.
  • As generic as possible - Re-use tools for multiple use cases.
  • Scales well - ABAP currently has 100+ object types. Even if it reaches 200+ object types the amount of MCP tools should stay the same e.g. one read tool for all objects, one tool for additional actions an object type might need (service binding needs a publish action), ...
  • Framework first - Most tools are built on frameworks and scale automatically e.g. the object creation tools do not need to be adjusted if a new object type gets introduced.
  • Solid out of the box experience - While AGENTS.md files can always be used to improve the performance of an agent, the tools shall work without any major custom instructions.
  • Integrates well with other MCP servers - The number one integration point between ABAP MCP servers are identifiers for objects. These can come in different types: name+type, URI, file path, ... Our server is built on the idea that the LLM can provide any valid identifier and the server does the mapping. This means community servers which might only offer one identifier work seamlessly with the ADT MCP server.

Supported tools

Tool IDDescriptionAdded with 1.2 release
abap_destination_listList available ABAP destinations 
abap_object_createCreate an ABAP object. Supports all object types which the new creation framework for VS Code supports 
abap_repository_list_creatable_typesList creatable object types 
abap_object_get_creatable_type_detailGet object metadata needed for creation 
abap_object_validate_creationValidate creation input 
abap_objects_generator_runGenerate objects 
abap_objects_generator_get_schemaGet generator schema 
abap_objects_generator_listList available generators 
abap_object_activateActivate ABAP objects 
abap_object_checkCheck ABAP objects for errorsYes
abap_object_list_actionsList available actions for an objectYes
abap_object_run_actionRun an action on an object. Besides actions which all objects support such as check, activate, lock, ... there are actions which are object type specific. One example is the service binding which has dedicated publish/unpublish actions. Currently, the service binding is the only object type which is already supported by the tool. In the future all object types will be supported.Yes
abap_object_get_document_symbolsSymbol map of a class/interface include. Basically the outline for a given object. It allows the LLM agent to first get a rough and token efficient overview before drilling down into the specificsYes
abap_object_read_fileRead an ABAP repository file. Supports all object types which can be natively viewed in ADT for EclipseYes
abap_object_edit_fileExact string replacement edit. Supports all object types which can be natively edited in ADT for EclipseYes
abap_object_get_aff_specificationGet AFF specification for an objectYes
abap_object_list_file_urisList AFF files of an object e.g. class includesYes
abap_object_get_file_uriConvert object name + type to file uriYes
abap_repository_search_objectSearch for development objectsYes
abap_transport_create_requestCreate a transport request 
abap_transport_get_requestGet/validate transport requests 
abap_transport_get_unified_diffUnified diff of a transport 
abap_unit_run_testsRun ABAP Unit tests 
abap_atc_run_get_resultGet ATC run result 
abap_atc_run_startStart an ATC run 
abap_atc_quickfixes_applyRun deterministic ATC quickfixes 
abap_atc_exemption_list_approversFind ATC exemption approversYes
abap_atc_exemption_requestCreate ATC exemption requestYes
abap_atc_ai_get_fix_resultCheck AI fix job status/result 
abap_atc_ai_start_fixApply AI fixes for ATC findings 
abap_business_service_get_infoFetch OData service info. Needed to build end-to-end Fiori applications in combination with the Fiori MCP server 
abap_business_service_listFetch services from a binding. Needed to build end-to-end Fiori applications in combination with the Fiori MCP server 
abap_feed_queryQuery an ABAP feed (FQL) e.g. shortdumps, gateway error logs, system messages, ...Yes
abap_feed_get_schemaGet ABAP feed schemaYes

Interoperability with other MCP servers or CLI tools

For all central ABAP development tasks such as CRUD support for objects or lifecycle management the official server should be the first choice. But the server will never satisfy all requirements and in this case additional servers or CLI tools are needed. This means the ADT MCP server needs to integrate nicely with the other solutions. The main integration point which we know is ABAP object IDs. A custom server might analyze an object and then want to use the ADT MCP server for reading additional object information. This needs to work seamlessly. Unfortunately, various forms of object IDs exist and we do not know which one is required. In order to solve this problem all our tools use a "oneOf" parameter which supports a range of object IDs.

Here the parameter description for the ABAP object identifier:

objectIdentifier (type oneOf): Identifies the ABAP object. Provide exactly one of:

- uri —> ADT URI (/sap/bc/adt/...), ADT Language Server URI, or SFS URI
- objectName + optional objectType —> e.g. CL_MY_CLASS with type CLAS
- affFileName —> AFF file name, e.g. cl_my_class.clas.abap

Recommended user journeys

How should an ABAP developer new to agentic development get started? The following paragraphs explain the recommended on-boarding path for such users.

Start with ADT for VS Code or ADT for Eclipse

From all the available options the user experience for ADT for VS Code is the most streamlined one.

  • The MCP server can be enabled with a single button click. No text based configuration needed.
  • All settings can be configured visually via the settings UI.
  • The chat UI makes it easy to configure the tools users need for their project.
  • The VS Code chat experience is polished and easy to use.

ADT for Eclipse is nearly as good. All settings can be done via a dedicated settings UI but the MCP server needs to be configured manually via a text based configuration.

For anybody who wants to experience agentic ABAP development for the first time the recommendation is to start with ADT for VS Code.

After the first steps connect the ADT for VS Code server to a CLI of your choice

 Here is a list of prominent CLIs:

  • Claude Code
  • OpenCode
  • Codex
  • GitHub Copilot CLI

All these CLIs work with the ADT MCP server. In order to enable the server a CLI specific configuration needs to be done. Just check the documentation for the respective CLI.

We recommend using the CLI next to your IDE. In this setup the MCP server process is attached to the IDE process. This setup allows developers to let agents run in the CLI and use the IDE to do code reviews, etc.

What's next?

Further development can be generally divided into two areas: 1) additional tools 2) refinement of existing tools. The following features are already planned. See roadmap for more information.

Refinement of existing tools

  • Support for coverage measurements when using the unit test run tool.
  • Improved destination tool. Providing additional metadata.
  • Improved object creation (adding missing object type support).
  • Improved read tool. Support of more extensibility artifacts.
  • ...

Additional tools

  • New source code search tool.
  • New where-used tool.
  • New tool for reading ABAP traces.
  • ...

Allow list improvements

Giving users the ability to provide individual settings for each destination.

Further information

  • Help page for the ADT MCP server
  • Roadmap information for ABAP AI related topics including the MCP server

entry.title: ABAP development tools for Visual Studio Code: Version 1.2 released
entry.content:
What happened since the last release?

Link to the extension.

Welcome back after the summer period! Hopefully you had a great time in the sun. We did not take a break and kept on working hard on the next version. It is available on the marketplace, now.

We heard your feedback. The additional object type support in version 1.1 made the extension a lot more useful for the ABAP developer community. With version 1.2 we continue this trend. It adds support for additional 23 object types. It features the first ABAP specific views and most importantly it updates the bundled MCP server with additional tools which will unlock the full power of all AI agents including Claude Code!

Some of you might wonder why this release took longer than the last ones. After the initial release we are now back to the regular three months rhythm that you know from ADT for Eclipse. It allows us to keep both products in sync and release new versions is parallel.

SAP TechEd Berlin is around the corner. We will have a demo station: „Build agents, workflows, and applications (AD)“. Stop by and have a chat. Let's talk VS Code, AI and how our tools can help you get things done!

 

What gets shipped with this release?

The following list only shows the major new additions. Of course, lots of smaller fixes, tweaks got added as well. See our what's new page for the full list.

Additional object type support

The following object types got added with full CRUD support:

Core ABAP
Transaction, Package, Software Components Relations, Transformation

CDS
Annotation Definition, Scalar Function Definition, Dynamic Cache, Static Cache, Entity Index

Data Dictionary
Data Element, Table technical settings

App Infrastructure 
Application Log Object, Archiving Object, Message Class, Background Processing Context, Application Job Catalog Entry, Application Job Template, Business Configuration Maintenance object

Fiori / UI
App Descriptor Item, Page Template, Space Template

Extensibility
BAdI Enhancement Spot, BAdI Enhancement Implementation, Predefined Field Enabling

The first ABAP specific views

Beyond pure object editors, the new release 1.2 brings several of the "classic" ADT views to VS Code for the first time.

Transport Organizer

First version of the transport organizer, so you can see and work with your transport requests without leaving VS Code.

ABAP feeds

First version of the feed reader for all available feeds such as short dumps, the gateway error log, system messages, ...

Timeline (Version history)

Lots of you requested this one. Version history view, letting you compare previous versions of an object.

SQL notebooks

A twist on the ADT for Eclipse SQL console. For VS Code we are integrating the SQL console using the VS Code notebook feature. It allows you to run ABAP SQL queries against the system database. Jupyter notebooks are a powerful concept. Make sure to look at the official VS Code documentation to get the most out of this integration.

Activation log

The activation log got refined, so you can inspect activation results and errors directly.

HANA source code search

If your system has the source code search enabled then the new command allows you to use it in VS Code.

Usability improvement for system connection handling

We received quite some feedback for this new option. Adding a new destination and tweaking the settings can now be done via a dedicated option for the "New Destination..." command. Previously, it required editing the destination file directly.

A major update of the bundled MCP server

The update is so BIG that we decided to create a separate blog for it! You can find it here.

 

What's next?

Have a look at our ABAP Cloud Roadmap page to see what comes next. Be aware that the MCP tools are getting listed under the AI section.

 

Provide feedback and influence our product backlog!

We welcome your feedback! Feel free to use the comment section or create a customer influence request to let us know which features you are missing the most. Your input will help us prioritize the feature backlog for the next releases.

entry.title: Implementing Print and Download PDF Features in SAP RAP Applications on S/4 HANA 2025 On-Premise
entry.content:
Introduction

One of the most common requirements when building SAP Fiori applications is providing users with a professional PDF document that can be downloaded, printed, archived, or attached to business processes.

In traditional SAP applications, this was often accomplished using Smart Forms or Adobe Forms. However, with SAP RAP (RESTful Application Programming Model), I wanted to implement this functionality and discovered that the solution spans multiple technologies:

  • Adobe LiveCycle Designer
  • CDS Form Data Providers (FDP)
  • Adobe Forms in ADT
  • RAP Actions
  • Fiori Extensions

This blog walks through the complete process of enabling "Print PDF" functionality directly from a RAP Object Page.

Solution Overview

The solution consists of thirteen major steps:

  1. Design the PDF layout
  2. Create the Form Data Provider CDS
  3. Create Access Control
  4. Expose the service
  5. Create the Adobe Form object
  6. Resolve ADT form runtime issues
  7. Generate XML for field binding
  8. Bind fields in Adobe Designer
  9. Finalize form design
  10. Upload updated XDP
  11. Validate the form
  12. Implement a RAP Action
  13. Download the PDF from Fiori


Step 1: Design the Form Layout

Create your form layout using Adobe LiveCycle Designer and save it as an XDP file. Do not worry about field bindings yet.
If Adobe LiveCycle Designer is not installed on your computer, it can be downloaded from the SAP Software Center:
Example: PDF form file name 'Z_MY_PDF_FORM'.

Step 2: Create a Form Data Provider CDS

The Adobe Form requires a CDS view to supply the data. The CDS must include the following annotation:

Example:

// https://help.sap.com/docs/abap-cloud/abap-development-tools-user-guide/creating-forms
@ObjectModel.supportedCapabilities: [ #OUTPUT_FORM_DATA_PROVIDER ]
define root view entity ZI_MY_PDF_DATA
provider contract transactional_query
  as select from ZR_MY_DATA
{
    key uuid,
    field1,
    field2,
    field3
}
This CDS acts as the Form Data Provider (FDP).
 

Step 3: Create Access Control

An often-overlooked requirement is that the Form Data Provider CDS must have an Access Control definition.
Example:

@EndUserText.label: 'PDF Data Access'
define role ZI_MY_PDF_DATA {
  grant select on ZI_MY_PDF_DATA
      where INHERITING CONDITIONS FROM ENTITY ZR_MY_DATA DEFAULT TRUE;
}

 

Step 4: Expose the CDS Service

Create a Service Definition and Service Binding.

define service ZUI_MY_PDF_SERVICE {
  expose ZI_MY_PDF_DATA;
}

Activate the service binding. This service will later be referenced by the Adobe Form object.


Step 5: Create the Adobe Form in ADT

In Eclipse ADT: (Note: Make sure ADT has been updated to at least 2026-06 version)

File
 └─ New
    └─ Other
       └─ Form Objects
          └─ Form

Provide:

  • Form Data Provider Service from Step # 4
  • XDP Layout File from Step # 1


Step 6: Address a Form Runtime Issue (Only affects On-Premise)

During implementation I encountered an issue where the form runtime required the ABAP language version to be adjusted for On-Premise scenario. SAP delivered code is expecting the scenario to only work for 'ABAP Cloud Development'.

In debugging, update:

SE16
 └─ FPCONTEXT
    └─ Search for your form name (Example: Z_MY_PDF_FORM)
       └─ In debug change the value of ABAP_LANGUAGE_VERSION = '5'
       └─ OR put an enhancement in 
          └─ Class: CL_FP_FORM_READER
             └─ Method: _check_form_language_version

Method is checking for value '5' which is for ABAP for Cloud Development 

--Note: SAP incident has been created to address this issue for On-Premise customer.

 

Step 7: Generate XML for Field Binding

One of the most useful techniques when working with Adobe Forms is generating XML directly from the Form Data Provider.

This XML can then be imported into Adobe LiveCycle Designer to simplify field binding.

The following utility code downloads a sample XML file:

  class-methods DOWNLOAD_XML_FOR_BINDING
    importing
      !IV_FORMNAME type FPNAME
      !IV_KEYS type IF_FP_FDP_API=>TT_SELECT_KEYS .
  METHOD download_xml_for_binding.
    DATA(form) = cl_fp_form_reader=>create_form_reader( iv_formname ).
    DATA(util) = cl_fp_fdp_services=>get_instance( form->get_fdp_name( ) ).
    DATA(keys) = util->get_keys( ).

    LOOP AT keys ASSIGNING FIELD-SYMBOL(<fs_key>).
      LOOP AT iv_keys INTO DATA(lv_key) WHERE name = <fs_key>-name.
        <fs_key>-value = lv_key-value.
      ENDLOOP.
    ENDLOOP.

    DATA(xml_string) =
      cl_abap_codepage=>convert_from(
        util->read_to_xml_v2( keys ) ).

    DATA(lt_xml_tab) = VALUE stringtab( ( xml_string ) ).
    CONSTANTS lc_sep TYPE c VALUE '\'.
    DATA(lv_filename) = |C:{ lc_sep }Users{ lc_sep }{ sy-uname }{ lc_sep }PDF{ lc_sep }{ iv_formname }.xml|.
    cl_gui_frontend_services=>gui_download(
      EXPORTING
        filename = lv_filename
        filetype = 'ASC'
      CHANGING
        data_tab = lt_xml_tab ).
  ENDMETHOD.

 

Step 8: Import XML into Adobe Designer

Inside Adobe LiveCycle Designer:

Field
 └─ Binding
      └─ New Data Connection
            └─ XML Schema

Upload the XML generated in the previous step. This automatically creates the available field structure for binding.

 

Step 9: Complete Field Binding

Bind all fields to the XML nodes generated from your CDS.  This is usually the most time-consuming part of form creation but becomes significantly easier with generated XML.

 

Step 10: Upload and Activate the Updated XDP

After completing the bindings:

  1. Save the XDP
  2. Return to ADT
  3. Upload the updated layout
  4. Activate the Adobe Form


Step 11: Validate the Form

Before integrating with RAP, validate both the FDP and Adobe Form.

A very useful utility provided by SAP is:

/sap/bc/http/sap/ZFDP_PREVIEWER_HTTP?sap-client=100

" Most likely you will not have the utility available in your system
Follow the instruction at 
https://sap-samples.github.io/forms-service-by-adobe-samples/preview_util.html
to put it in your system

The utility allows you to:

  • Validate field mappings
  • Test CDS output
  • Preview PDF generation
  • Troubleshoot rendering issues

This utility helped me resolve several binding issues long before testing through the Fiori application.

 

Step 12: Implement a RAP Action

Next, create a RAP action that renders the PDF and returns it to the frontend.

Example:

--Behavior definition:
action ( features : instance ) PreviewPDF result [1] z_print_pdf;

-- PDF output
@EndUserText.label: 'PDF Output'
define abstract entity z_print_pdf
{
  filecontent : abap.string;
  filename    : abap.string;
  mimetype    : abap.string;
}
--Behavior Implementation:
METHODS PreviewPDF FOR MODIFY
IMPORTING keys FOR ACTION ZR_MY_DATA~PreviewPDF RESULT result.

METHOD PreviewPDF.
    DATA: lv_fileName TYPE string.
    LOOP AT keys ASSIGNING FIELD-SYMBOL(<key>).
      CLEAR: lv_fileName.
      READ ENTITIES OF ZR_MY_DATA IN LOCAL MODE
        ENTITY MyData
        FIELDS (
          field1
          field2
	  field3
        )
      WITH VALUE #( ( %tky = <key>-%tky ) )
      RESULT DATA(lt_review).

      IF sy-subrc <> 0.
        CONTINUE.
      ELSE.
        DATA(ls_review) = lt_review[ 1 ].
      ENDIF.

      lv_filename = |{ ls_review-field1 }_{ ls_review-field2 }_{ ls_review-field3 }.pdf|.

	  "Wrap below with try/catch and handle exceptions
	  DATA(form) = cl_fp_form_reader=>create_form_reader( CONV #( |Z_MY_PDF_FORM| ) ).
	  DATA(util) = cl_fp_fdp_services=>get_instance( form->get_fdp_name( ) ).
	  DATA(pdfKeys) = util->get_keys( ).
		  
      pdfKeys[ name = 'UUID' ]-value = <key>-uuid. " UUID is the key field in CDS that returns data for the form
	  
	  DATA(xml) = util->read_to_xml_v2( pdfkeys ).
	  cl_fp_ads_util=>render_pdf(
		  EXPORTING
			  iv_locale       = 'en_US'
			  iv_xdp_layout   = form->get_layout( )
			  iv_xml_data     = xml
			  is_options      = VALUE #(
				  "0 - only errors <= intended for production
				  "4 - very detailed trace <= intended for development
				  trace_level = 0
				  embed_fonts = form->get_font_embed( ) )
		  IMPORTING
			  ev_pdf          = DATA(pdf)
			  ev_trace_string = DATA(logs)
	  ).
      DATA(xpdf) = cl_web_http_utility=>encode_x_base64( pdf ).

      REPLACE ALL OCCURRENCES OF '-' IN xpdf WITH '+'.
      REPLACE ALL OCCURRENCES OF '_' IN xpdf WITH '/'.

      CONDENSE xpdf NO-GAPS.

      APPEND VALUE #( %cid_ref = <key>-%cid_ref
                      uuid       = <key>-uuid
                      %param   = VALUE z_print_pdf(
                                    filecontent = xpdf
                                    mimetype = |application/pdf|
                                    filename = lv_filename
                                    )
                       )
             TO result.
    ENDLOOP.
  ENDMETHOD.
The generated PDF is Base64 encoded and returned through the RAP action result structure.
 

Step 13: Download the PDF in Fiori

The final step is a Fiori extension that:

  1. Invokes the RAP action
  2. Receives the Base64 content
  3. Creates a browser Blob
  4. Downloads the PDF

User experience:

Manifest.jsons
   |
   +-- Add custom action to trigger the RAP Action
                  "actions": {
                    "ObjectPageExtension": {
                      "press": "<yourdomain>.ext.controller.ObjectPageExtension.onShowPDF",
                      "requiresSelection": false,
                      "icon": "sap-icon://print",
                      "text": "Print"
                    }
                  },

Object Page Controller Extension
   |
   +-- Download PDF (This code can be better)
 onShowPDF: async function (
            oBindingContext,
            aSelectedContexts
        ) {
            try {
                BusyIndicator.show(0);
                const aResult =
                    await this.editFlow.invokeAction(
                        "com.sap.gateway.srvd.<yourservice>.PreviewPDF",
                        {
                            contexts: [oBindingContext],
                            grouping: "Isolated"
                        }
                    );
                const oReturnContext = aResult[0].value;

                // Read the action result payload
                const oActionResult =
                    await oReturnContext.requestObject();
                if (
                    !oActionResult ||
                    !oActionResult.filecontent
                ) {
                    MessageBox.error(
                        "No PDF returned from PreviewPDF action."
                    );
                    return;
                }
                let sBase64 = oActionResult.filecontent;
                const sFileName = oActionResult.filename || "MyData.pdf";
                const sMimeType = oActionResult.mimetype || "application/pdf";
                // Convert Base64URL to Base64
                sBase64 = sBase64
                    .replace(/-/g, "+")
                    .replace(/_/g, "/");
                // Restore required padding
                while (sBase64.length % 4 !== 0) {
                    sBase64 += "=";
                }
                // Decode
                const sBinary = window.atob(sBase64);
                const aBytes = new Uint8Array(sBinary.length);
                for (let i = 0; i < sBinary.length; i++) {
                    aBytes[i] = sBinary.charCodeAt(i);
                }
                const oBlob = new Blob(
                    [aBytes],
                    {
                        type: sMimeType
                    }
                );
                const sBlobUrl = URL.createObjectURL(oBlob);
                const link = document.createElement("a");
                link.href = sBlobUrl;
                link.download = sFileName;
                document.body.appendChild(link);
                link.click();
                document.body.removeChild(link);
                setTimeout(() => {
                    URL.revokeObjectURL(sBlobUrl);
                }, 1000);              
            }
            catch (oError) {

                console.error(
                    oError
                );
                MessageBox.error(
                    oError?.message ||
                    "Error generating PDF."
                );
            }
            finally {
                BusyIndicator.hide();
            }
        }


Conclusion

While SAP RAP modernizes application development, generating professional PDF documents still requires integration with Adobe Forms.

By combining:

  • CDS Form Data Providers
  • Adobe Forms in ADT
  • RAP Actions
  • SAP Fiori Extensions

you can deliver a seamless PDF generation experience directly from a RAP Object Page or on List report page. This solution seems good and in alignment with RAP programming model. If you have suggestions to make it better or alternative approaches to achieve the requirement then please share your feedback in the comments.
